thus, it is said that they are "identical to sound. An opponent asks: "If names and so forth are identical to sound, what would be the respective objects of the two analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)—that of phenomena (*dharma*) and that of eloquence (*nirukti*)?"

They are distinct. Therefore, the treatise answers: "Because these factors—dharma, expression, and arrival—are each different, it is precisely by taking these as objects that the two spheres of cognition differ.

The analytical knowledge of dharma (dharmapratisaṃvid) takes conventional designations (prajñapti) and so forth as its object; the analytical knowledge of expression (niruktipratisaṃvid) takes actual sounds (śabda) and so forth as its object."

Therefore, it is said that there is a distinction between their objects. It is not the case that both take the reality as their object. Although the two natures are mutually inseparable, because the *dharma* (the teaching) corresponds to what is expressed (*vācya*), it is called "name" (*nāman*) alone;
because the *pada* (the phrase) mostly corresponds to the capacity of the listener (*yogya*), it is called "sound" (*ghoṣa*) alone.

Since the ear hears the sound and thereby fully comprehends the meaning, the two are said to differ because of their different respective objects, not because there is a difference in their essence. Furthermore:
Regarding the distinction between these two objects and the three—names (*nāman*) and so forth—from sound (*śabda*):

since their inclusion within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) also differs, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the base of sound (*śabdāyatana*), and the element of sound (*śabdadhātu*) belong exclusively to sound; whereas the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) belong to names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*).

Question: If the metaphorical designation (*prajñapti*) based on the curvature of sound is not associated with speech (*vāk-saṃprayukta*), then by analogy, the metaphorical designation based on the curvature of form should also [not be associated with matter].
"It is not included within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). He answers: "In sound there is informative intimation (*vijñapti*), whereas in form there is no informative intimation;
therefore, it is included within the sphere of form. Again he asks: "If there is curvature in sound, it constitutes an instruction (*śāsana*);

if there were curvature in form as well, it too should constitute an instruction. Therefore, the Master of the Treatise answers: "For now, this is explained according to the conventions of this land."

Regarding the statement that "phrases, words, and phonemes are established as three [categories]," this reconciles apparent contradictions. That is to say, it is based on this [Saha] world-system that the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes are conventionally established in dependence upon sound;
it does not mean that they are likewise established in dependence upon sound in all other realms and worlds. Question:
In what do the other realms and worlds depend for their establishment? Answer: In all other Buddha-fields, they are likewise established in dependence upon light, as well as subtle odors and tastes.

...and so forth. The collections of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) are provisionally established because one can discern meanings through those [objects] such as visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
This refers to what is cited from the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*. As for the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes tangibles, mental volition (*manasikāra*), and so on.
All of the above are capable of being provisionally established as the three types—names and so forth—and they are also subsumed under the category of dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
It is because of three factors. It is provisional (*upāya*) because it is established in relation to the capacities and inclinations of sentient beings.
Furthermore, in Sanskrit it is called *vyañjana*. This has four meanings: first, a fan; second, the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); third, the sense organs and forms; and fourth, flavor.

This refers to salt, for it can manifest the flavors within various substances. "Flavor" here refers to literary expression (*vyañjana*), as in the phrase "the elegance of words and meaning," which is what this term denotes.
For the sake of convenience, the four meanings herein are collectively termed "manifestation" (*vyañjana*). The ancient masters explain this as "flavor" (*rasa*). The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states:
"This is called 'manifestation' because it can manifest that meaning; thus, it serves as the basis for names and phrases, as it is able to manifest the meaning.
*Akṣara* is "syllable" (*pada*); it has the sense of being unalterable. As the *Abhidharma* says: "A *bha*... [and so forth].
The *pada* (footstep) is like seeking an elephant by following its tracks; this is what is called a "phrase" (*pada*). Logically, it should be called a "trace," for it is the trace of meaning.
By following this, one comes to know the meaning. Following the ancient translations, it is termed a "phrase."

There are those who maintain that the *anuśaya* (latent dispositions) are distinct from the mind and mental factors; [this view], following the same principles as previously established, should be refuted.

Seventh, the refutation of other views regarding the *anuśaya*: they assert that the *anuśaya* are themselves afflictive mental factors such as greed (*lobha*). "Anu" (following) has the meaning of arising together with; "śaya" (lying down/sleeping) has the meaning of a seed.
That is to say, the seeds of the afflictions follow along with sentient beings and lie dormant within the *ālayavijñāna*. This is their position.
[The opponent claims that] they are subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*). Therefore, the Master [Vasubandhu] refutes this, saying:

"Since the seeds of greed and so forth are called 'greed' and so forth, they must necessarily be associated with a defiled mind, just like the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of greed and so forth. How can they be called 'dissociated'?

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) you maintain are not dissociated from mind, because they are named after greed and so forth, just like the manifest greed and so forth.
There are other dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), namely the ten dharmas not yet refuted:

namely, flux (*pravṛtti*), distinctness (*anyathātva*), association (*samyoga*), velocity (*java*), succession (*anukrama*), time (*kāla*), direction (*deśa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), cohesion (*sāmagrī*), and non-cohesion (*asāmagrī*).

"According to the preceding reasoning" means according to the reasoning of the fourteen dharmas previously refuted. "To exclude" means to exclude [the existence of] something distinct from matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
[They] maintain that there is a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) [to these].
All unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are apart from matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth—meaning they are apart from the real unconditioned nature of matter, mind, and so forth.

The three unconditioned phenomena are divided into three parts. First is the general refutation; first, a general censure: "Now, to establish that they exist," and so forth, is intended for the purpose of refutation.
Regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): first, taking the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as an example, the number is first indicated and then explained in detail below.

As for "such as form and mind," this refers to the objects of the five groups of sensory consciousnesses and the knowledge of others' minds—namely, the five sense-objects such as form, as well as the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

This is stated in terms of their collective aggregation; it does not specifically distinguish which particular consciousness they are the objects of. They are what is known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), not what is known through [inferential] objects.

Regarding "such as jars, clothes, and so forth": although these are currently seen and utilized, they are not objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they are conventional (*prajñapti*) phenomena;

they are merely things being utilized in the present. Question: Within this context, what type of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does the mind that takes jars and so forth as its object belong to? Answer: It is subsumed under non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).

This is because it does not directly apprehend the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the phenomenon, nor is it an inference (*anumāna*). It is not [non-valid] in the sense of being a misconception, but rather because it lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge.

"Subsumed under valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). 'Established without depending on reasons' means that these two dharmas are not established by means of inference (*anumāna*) based on a thesis (*pakṣa*) and a reason (*hetu*), because they are known to exist through common consensus, like the eye, ear, and so forth.
This refers to the fact that these five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) are not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, these eyes, ears, and so forth are not commonly known by people of the present day; rather, their existence is inferred through the fact that each possesses the function of generating consciousness.
The term "realized knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) refers to the principle of logical proof (*upapatti-sādhana*), because the cause is inferred from the direct perception of its effect.

The "effect" refers to the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) that are produced; through this inference (*anumāna*), one knows that the various pure material faculties (*rūpa-indriya*) exist.

This is not established by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the knowledge of others' minds. However, the object of the eighth consciousness in the Mahāyāna is also apprehended through direct perception;

when the Buddha’s wisdom takes it as its object, it is likewise apprehended through direct perception. Apart from the Buddha, this is accepted as a matter of common scholarly consensus, rather than being something universally known to the world.
Therefore, it is said that its existence is known through inference (*anumāna*). If it were unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it would not be something known through direct perception.

Dharma. Furthermore, it is not a dharma that possesses functional activity (for that which is currently being experienced is a conventional dharma; here we are merely refuting that the unconditioned is not real, and thus do not distinguish between them).

Even if one were to grant that it possesses functional activity, it would necessarily be impermanent. How, then, can one insist that the unconditioned definitely exists? However, the passage beginning with "But all... correctly reveals the meaning that the unconditioned is not real.
As for "the nature of the knowable," this refers to the comprehension [of the unconditioned] derived from hearing the name "unconditioned" spoken.
Within the mind, one takes up the nature of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). As for this manifested nature:

when the conditioned phenomena of form and mind—whose meanings as cause and effect are exhausted, or whose conditions are lacking—no longer possess the meaning of being conditioned, they manifest as unconditioned.

Thus, these natures, both the cognized and the manifested, such as form and mind, are all impermanent; therefore, it is incorrect to cling to them as existing substantially apart from the mind. The formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are existent dharmas. One should not maintain the thesis that they are a truly existent unconditioned nature distinct from form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth;
for the reasons stated: because they are objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), or because their nature is manifested by form, mind, and so forth. The analogy is like form, mind, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding whether space and so forth are one or many (up to the point where it is argued they should not exist as something distinct from the mind and its contents, like a rabbit’s horn), there is a second refutation.
These are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). According to various sūtras and śāstras, there are generally six types.
First, the unconditioned phenomenon of space (*ākāśa-asaṃskṛta*) is the true reality manifested by being free from the obstructions of all phenomena of form and mind; this is called space.

As for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there are three kinds of space (*ākāśa*): first, space as a transformation of consciousness, which refers to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of space that arises through the interpretive mind within the six consciousnesses;
second, space as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-ākāśa*), which refers to the essence of true suchness (*tathatā*) itself, so called because it is free from all obstructions;
and third, substantial space (*vastu-ākāśa*), which refers to the insentient, empty void that is perceived. Second, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This refers to the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) manifested through the elimination of all obstructive defilements by means of discernment arising from untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

Third is the unconditioned cessation not through discernment (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*). This refers to those phenomena that are inherently pure by nature, even without the power of discernment arising from untainted wisdom;
this is precisely the nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa*), which is the very nature of True Suchness, free from all [defilements].

1. The unconditioned state of the cessation of obscurations and defilements (*āvaraṇa-kleśa-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*): because its essential nature is pure, it does not depend on the arising of wisdom to sever delusions.

2. The unconditioned state of immovability (*aniñjya-asaṃskṛta*): in the fourth dhyāna, one is free from the eight afflictions and the three calamities; thus, one realizes the unconditioned state of immovability. 3.

The unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*): from the levels above the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), neither neutral sensation nor coarse perception functions.
It is also non-existent. That which reveals the attainment of *tathatā* (suchness) is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Regarding the six unconditioned states of *tathatā*, there are two [meanings]: first, that which is named in relation to its counterpart; this refers to the principle of *tathatā*, which receives its name in contrast to conditioned phenomena (*dharma*). Second, that which distinguishes the dharma;

this refers to *tathatā* itself, which distinguishes itself from the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and is free from arising and ceasing. Other vehicles only admit the first three types, which are devoid of form (*rūpa*).
The mind and so forth possess a real intrinsic nature; this has already been refuted by means of the analysis into unity and plurality.
Furthermore, regarding space and so forth—“and so forth” (etc. including the other two types—is its nature one or many? If its nature were one, the fault of a single entity would follow;
if its nature were many, the fault of multiple entities would follow. Within the initial refutation of the fault of a single entity, the passage beginning with “Space contains... refutes space.

"Not one. Under the section "One Part, One Chapter, Lower": refuting that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not one. Under the section "The Absence of Conditions for a Single Dharma, Lower":
refuting that non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not one. "If its essence were one and pervasive throughout all places"—this indicates the tenet held by that school.
"If space were unable to contain form and so forth, how could it be called 'space'? Since it is indeed able to contain form and so forth, then...
If [space] were to merge with form and other phenomena to become one, then since form and the others are manifold, the substance of space would also have to be manifold;
how then can it be said to be one? At the place where it merges with one phenomenon, it does not merge with all others; how then can it be said to pervade all locations?
If it did not merge with one phenomenon but merged with others, then all phenomena would necessarily interpenetrate one another, because of space...

Because space completely enters into all phenomena (*dharma*). If one were to claim that space is a single entity which does not combine with various phenomena but unites with only a single phenomenon, then space would be unable to contain [all things], just like other unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), because other unconditioned phenomena cannot encompass all phenomena.
The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: "The unconditioned phenomenon of space is a subject (*dharmin*); it ought to..."
This is not an acceptable tenet. The reason is given: "Because it does not conjoin with phenomena," with the example being "like other unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, is there space within form and so forth? If there is, then space and form would be intermingled and indistinguishable; if there is not, then space and form would be separated and [space] would not be pervasive.

Next, using *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) and *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation) as examples, he refutes [the opponent's position], saying: "If they were of a single essence, then it should..."

When one abandons a single category (prakāra) of a single group (nikāya) of fetters (saṃyojana), one does not merely attain the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of that specific category and group; rather, one attains the analytical cessation of all other categories and all other groups.
Furthermore, when a single phenomenon (dharma) fails to arise due to the absence of conditions, one does not merely attain the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of that one phenomenon;

one should attain the non-analytical cessation of all phenomena. Why? Because according to their [opponent's] tenet, the essence (svabhāva) of these cessations is one; thus, if it were one, [the attainment of one would entail the attainment of all].

This refers to all [of them]. It is logically necessary that it be so; thus, the conclusion is reached. This fetter is a defilement of volition (*cetanā-kleśa*) consisting of eighty-one grades, which are distributed among nine categories.

These nine categories correspond to the nine stages (*bhūmi*). Later, the fault of "multiple entities" (*aneka-svabhāva-doṣa*) is raised, stating: "If the substance of space and so forth were multiple..."
The thesis is that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not ultimately real. The reason is: "because it possesses distinct categories. The example is: "like form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, the thesis is that space (*ākāśa*) does not universally contain all things. The reason is: "because it possesses distinct categories. The example is: "like form and so forth.

One should understand that *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) and *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation) are treated accordingly. Below this, the total demonstration is that the unconditioned as asserted by other schools is not real.
"There are [unconditioned phenomena] held by other schools; namely, the latter three types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). These should be refuted according to the previous [arguments].

This means that one should further interrogate them based on the preceding examples, such as existence and non-existence. Furthermore, a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is set forth to refute them in general: "The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that the various unconditioned phenomena are not distinct from mind and so forth.
The reason (*hetu*) is: because they are admitted to lack cause and effect. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like a rabbit's horn."
However, since the sūtras state that there are such things as space (ākāśa), etc., [it follows that] the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas are not necessarily substantially real.

Third, the elucidation of the correct meaning: first, regarding those that are provisionally established based on the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*). This refers to their essential nature being produced through the transformation of consciousness.

This refers to the unconditioned state of emptiness (*śūnyatā-asamskṛta*). From the outset, it lacks any intrinsic essence; it is merely a transformation of the mind, like an infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇu*), which is provisional and devoid of substantiality.
Because one hears its name from the Buddha and others, the mind transforms accordingly.

Through the power of repeated cultivation and refinement upon hearing the teachings on the five kinds of unconditioned phenomena, such as emptiness, when the various consciousnesses arise, they transform and manifest as semblances or reflections of emptiness and the rest.

The image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) serves as the objective referent (ālambana). This manifested image remains similar from one moment to the next, without undergoing change, because it consists solely of a single class of characteristics such as space;
therefore, it is conventionally designated as "permanent. If, however, one speaks of the essential nature (svabhāva) as being unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), [then it is permanent].
This means that it does not exist apart from the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*). Question:

If one says that the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect) of the transformation of consciousness is explained as being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), then since it is merely a characteristic mark that functions in accordance with consciousness, how can it be established as unconditioned? Answer: This is said to be the transformation of consciousness;
it is provisionally designated as unconditioned, but in reality it is not unconditioned. Unconditioned phenomena are eternally abiding (*nitya*).

Regarding the Dharma [nature]: that which here relies on the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) essence takes as its essence only the "solitary shadow-image" (pratibimba) aspect that accords with consciousness.

Because it is similar and unchanging, it is metaphorically described as "permanent. These six unconditioned phenomena, when transformed by the consciousness of a Bodhisattva prior to the stages (bhūmi), are contaminated (sāsrava);
if they are transformed by the subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) of one on the stages, they are uncontaminated (anāsrava). Second, the basis.

Regarding the statement that "the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is provisionally established": this establishes its essence based on the nature of phenomena. The five kinds of unconditioned phenomena are all suchness (tathatā);
outside the essence of suchness, there is nothing else that arises. Each of the six kinds of unconditioned phenomena is based upon the actual qualities of suchness.
This essence must be realized only after one has attained the realization of the two emptinesses—of persons and of phenomena—and the absence of self; only then does it become manifest.
To say it exists is to fall into the slander of superimposition (*samāropa*). To say it does not exist is to fall into the slander of denial (*apavāda*).

To say it both exists and does not exist is to fall into the slander of contradiction. To say it neither exists nor does not exist is to fall into the slander of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Therefore, it is said that it is neither existent nor non-existent; the mind wishes to take it as an object, yet deliberation vanishes; the mouth wishes to speak of it, yet words fail. Thus, it is called the "path beyond mind and speech."

They are distinct in terms of nature and characteristics; therefore, they are said to be "not one. They are identical in terms of nature and identical in terms of characteristics; therefore, they are said to be "not different.
Because it is the nature of phenomena, it is called "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*). Because it is free from all obstructions, it is called "space" (*ākāśa*).

As for "analytical cessation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is also named "cessation through deliberation" (*saṃkhyāya nirodha*). "Deliberation" refers to the factor of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*); by taking wisdom as the condition, one discriminates among the various afflictions and is thus able to manifest the principle of cessation.

Therefore, the Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty translated it as "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Cessation attained by the power of discernment is called "cessation through discernment," just as a cart drawn by oxen is called an "ox-cart.

This has the nature of dissociation (*visamyoga*); by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one cuts off all obstructive defilements, becomes detached from bondage, and realizes liberation, which is conventionally designated as "cessation through discernment. As for "cessation not through discernment" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)...
It is also called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). It is not obtained by the extinction of afflictions through the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*);

rather, it is manifested through intrinsic purity and the absence of conditions. Regarding the "absence of conditions," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "That which absolutely obstructs what is to arise."

One separately attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The commentary explains: "That which is to arise" refers to dharmas that are destined to arise in the future. When conditions assemble, they arise; when conditions are lacking, they do not arise.
At the time of this non-arising, one attains non-analytical cessation. This non-analytical cessation obstructs those dharmas that are to arise.
To cause [a phenomenon] never to arise again is called "ultimate obstruction" (*atyantavighna*). Regarding the term "distinct acquisition" (*prāpti-viśeṣa*):

it means that non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) possesses a real ontological characteristic, because a distinct acquisition arises during the state when conditions are absent. The acquisition of non-analytical cessation does not depend on analytical cessation;

rather, it is called non-analytical cessation simply because of the absence of conditions. As the treatise points out a specific case to clarify this: for example, when the eye and the mind are focused exclusively on a single form (*rūpa*).

When other objects—such as visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—have ceased, the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) that take those objects as their conditions remain in the future and never arise.
Because they are unable to take past objects as their conditions—the necessary conditions being incomplete—they attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The commentary states: when the eye takes a visible form as its object, it is also capable of taking sounds and so forth as its objects; however, because it is focused exclusively on the visible form [it does not arise].

The ear and other [senses] do not take sound and other [objects] as their conditions, because by the time [the sense organ would encounter them], the momentary sound and so forth have already passed away;
thus, the consciousnesses that take sound and so forth as their objects do not arise again.

Since the first five consciousnesses only take present objects as their conditions and do not take past or future ones, the phrase "contact and so forth" includes those among the dharmas that exist simultaneously with the perceiving faculty and serve as its objective condition (*ālambana*), such as...
This is the object of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). This knowledge of others' minds takes only the present mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as its object;

it should also take mental factors (*caitta*) as its objects, yet because it focuses exclusively on the mind-king, it does not attain the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding mental factors. As for "immovability" (*āniñjya*):

having departed from the first three dhyānas, one reaches the fourth dhyāna; having departed from the three calamities, one escapes the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), and is devoid of joy, pleasure, and so forth.
The truth manifested by the shaking of body and mind is called "immovable cessation" (*aniñjya-nirodha*). As for the "cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*):

it refers to one who has already abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and transcended the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). Preceded by mental attention (*manasikāra*), they temporarily bring to rest perception;

thus, there is the cessation of the non-permanent mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), as well as the cessation of a portion of the permanent mental states and mental factors. This is the truth manifested thereby.

Regarding the principle that the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha*) is also a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), it means that although *tathatā* (suchness) is expressed through linguistic conventions, the essence of what is expressed is one and the same.
These five unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are provisionally named "emptiness" and so forth based upon *tathatā*;

however, the essence of *tathatā* is neither like [anything] nor unlike [anything]. Therefore, even the name "*tathatā*" is a provisional construction. It is like the term for an "oil-eating insect," which does not [correspond to a literal reality].
Regarding its essence: the word "only" (eva) is used to indicate this. For example, there is an insect called "oil-eater," yet it does not actually eat oil because that is not its true nature.
True Suchness (*tathatā*) is likewise: to those who hold the view of emptiness as a mere void, it is described as "existent";

to prevent the Mahīśāsaka school and others within the Hīnayāna from clinging to it as a fixed, substantial reality, it is described as "empty. This does not mean that the essence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is itself non-existent.
Furthermore, do not say that "empty" and "illusory" refer to the same thing. "Empty" excludes the *parikalpita* (imagined nature), while "illusory" excludes the *paratantra* (dependent nature);
this reveals that *tathatā* (suchness) is the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature). Because it is devoid of false and inverted phenomena, it is named "Suchness.
Thus, the *Zongjing lu* says: Question: How does the holy teaching describe Suchness as real? Answer: What we now call "existent" is not [the ultimate] reality.
If one says that names exist substantially and merely asserts their existence, this is precisely the rejection of a wrongly grasped emptiness (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*).

Therefore, it is said that having an essence is the wondrously existent true emptiness; thus, it is described as "neither empty nor existent. Question: How is it that the holy teachings describe *tathatā* (suchness) as empty? Answer:
It is said to be empty in order to refute the attachment that conceives of *tathatā* as existing as a real entity external to the mind; thus, it empties that very mental clinging.
[This refers to] grasping at the essence of non-empty *tathatā*. This concludes the two preceding refutations of the other vehicles (*yāna*).

Regarding the various phenomena grasped by outsiders (*tīrthika*) and those of the other vehicles—as far as [the claim that] grasping at external objects is also grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Third, the general refutation. This concludes the refutation of the non-Buddhists' and other vehicles' clinging to dharmas. Just as in the case of the refutation of the clinging to a self (*ātman-grāha*), a formal inference (*prayoga*) is established to refute them generally.
In that [previous] case, the capacity (the subject) was stated first and the object (the predicate) last;

here, the object is stated first and the capacity last, because the self belongs to the faculties while dharmas belong to the objects. The various dharmas grasped as distinct from mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are the *dharmin* (the subject) of the thesis. It is not...

The "existence as a real entity" is the predicate (dharmin) of the subsequent thesis. The reason (*hetu*) states: "Because it is an apprehended object consisting of a conceptualized image-part (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "like the mind and mental factors. Furthermore, the cognition that apprehends those phenomena is also not [directly] taking those phenomena as its object; this is the thesis. The reason states: [Because it is a conceptualized image-part].
This is because it is the aspect of the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*). It is analogous to the cognition that takes this very [subject-aspect] as its object.

That is to say, when the sixth consciousness perceives a conventional phenomenon (*prajñapti-dharma*), its conventional objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) arises solely through the transformation of the subject-aspect; it possesses no seeds of its own, nor does it rely upon an external substantial reality (*bimba*).
This is termed "solitary shadow" (*kevala-chāyā*), which arises solely from the subject-aspect. Therefore, the mind and mental factors take this cognition as their object.
This serves as a homologous example (*sapakṣa*). This is the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Since it has already been clarified that [entities] distinct from mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) do not possess a real intrinsic nature (*dravyasat*), there is a fear that people might consequently cling to the view that all minds and mental factors do possess a real intrinsic nature; therefore, the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is set forth:
All minds and mental factors are phenomena that exist; it is our thesis that they do not exist as ultimate reality. The reason is: because they are dependently originated.
The example is: like illusory phenomena. Should someone ask: "If all minds and mental factors are not substantially real, why does the teaching state that 'there is only consciousness'?
To this, we reply: It is for the purpose of dispelling the attachments of non-Buddhists and followers of other vehicles to a [self] separate from the mind.

Mental factors have distinct, real objects. Therefore, it is said in the teachings that there is "consciousness-only. If one were to hold that consciousness-only truly exists, this would be no different from the false attachment to external objects as being real;
it would likewise constitute the clinging to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*). For this reason, [it is taught that even consciousness-only is empty].
One should simply eliminate the objects external to that mind, which are non-existent like the horns of a rabbit; the cognizing mind itself exists like a magical illusion.
Thus, there is a slight difference [between them], but this does not mean that the mind itself is also called substantially existent. Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
The establishment of the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) was originally intended to eliminate both objects and mind.

Now that objects are non-existent and consciousness itself has also subsided, this signifies the completion of the realization of the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra*. This is because both the afflictions and their objects—which constitute the category of the impure—have equally ceased to exist.

Question: One may rightly call it the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* when objects are eliminated while consciousness remains; however, since both object and consciousness have been eliminated, how can this still be termed *vijñapti-mātra*?
Which consciousness can be established? Answer: The establishment of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is, at first, a provisional method of discarding the object while retaining the mind.

However, this is ultimately for the purpose of the treatise: by discarding the object, one seeks to empty the mind; thus, both object and consciousness are extinguished. This is its correct principle.

This extinction of both object and consciousness is itself the true nature (*tathatā*). This true nature is the *amala-vijñāna* (immaculate consciousness). As the ancient masters said: "It is like perceiving the Truth."

If one conceives of "suchness" (tathatā) as having existence, this is attachment to phenomena (dharmagrāha). If one conceives of it as non-existence, although this does not accord with suchness, one nevertheless becomes a sage by means of that cause.

The commentary states: If one conceives of suchness as having existence, this is attachment to phenomena; if one gives rise to a mind that understands [it], one thereby establishes the principle that is realized.
Once the objective realm is established, the mind is deluded regarding direct perception (pratyakṣa); as soon as cognition and understanding arise, [the mind is already lost].

This constitutes an inference that would forfeit the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra). Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states: "Outside of wisdom there is no suchness for wisdom to enter;
outside of suchness there is no wisdom capable of realizing suchness. Thus, mind and object are suchness (tathatā), a single path of purity.

However, there are briefly two types of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). [From "up to" *dharmagrāha*] the true suchness of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatātathatā*) is that which can eliminate them.

Fourth, this is a general summary of pervasive attachments. Regarding the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*): in the teachings, form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are distinguished within a single moment of thought.
Taking form and mind as they are, one opens them into the five aggregates (*skandhas*). Taking form-objects and mind as they are, one opens them into the twelve bases (*āyatanas*).
Furthermore, taking the five aggregates as they are, one opens them into the eighteen elements (*dhātus*). In the five aggregates, form is combined into one, while mind is opened into four;

this is established for those who are deluded regarding mind but not regarding form. In the twelve bases, mind is combined into one half (in contrast to the previous opening into four, it is now said to be "combined," meaning the mental base [manāyatana] in its entirety).

And a portion of the *dharmāyatana*. Master Kai said: "That which is apprehended by the mind is called 'dharma. There are four categories within the *dharmāyatana*: first, mental factors (*caitta*); second, formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*); third, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*); and fourth, non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*). Here, it refers to a portion of the mental factors; therefore, it is called 'half'.

To divide form (*rūpa*) into ten and a half [categories] (in contrast to the previous grouping where form was treated as one, this is the "division": namely, the five objects—form, sound, odor, taste, and touch—and the five sense organs—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—constituting ten; the term "half" refers to the non-informative matter within the *dharmāyatana*).
This was established for those who are deluded regarding form but not regarding the mind. [The eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) concern the mind.]

The simultaneous opening of both form and mind (meaning that form is opened into ten-and-a-half [categories], as previously the mind was opened into seven-and-a-half; namely, the six consciousnesses as six, plus the mental faculty, the dharma-base, and the mental factors) is established for the sake of those who are deluded regarding both mind and form.
All of these are merely provisional designations; how could there be any real dharmas to be grasped?
Because the objects of perception may be opened or closed, the perceiving subject likewise may be either general or specific. This attachment to dharmas is like the previous attachment to a self.

Regarding the two types of grasping (*grāha*), if one distinguishes them according to the Mahāyāna, the two types of conceptual grasping (*vikalpita-grāha*) are abandoned all at once at the first moment of the first stage (*bhūmi*).

As for the two types of innate grasping (*sahaja-grāha*), one portion of each is abandoned in each successive stage, until the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāpatti-jñāna*), where two remaining delusions (*moha*) still persist.

These are finally and instantaneously exhausted at the final moment of the Vajra-like Samādhi. Therefore it is said: "Conceptual grasping of self and phenomena is absent in the Stage of Extreme Joy; the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] are both [abandoned]."

The ground of birth and the ground of the stages are eliminated. At the seventh stage, through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the seeds are eliminated; once the Vajra-like Samādhi is manifested, all subsequent [afflictions] are likewise non-existent.

If one follows the Hīnayāna perspective, at the time of the initial Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one suddenly severs the conceptual grasping at a self (*parikalpita-ātma-grāha*) and immediately realizes the first fruit (*phala*).

By exhausting the innate [grasping at a self], one then realizes the fourth fruit. However, the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is not included therein. As for the characteristics of the "self-nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth, these belong to the Sāṃkhya school.
The primordial darkness (*āṇḍa*), the primal nature (*prakṛti*), and other such categories grasped by others may be understood through the same principle as the aforementioned attachment to a self.
Thus, it is said that all attachments to phenomena (up to the point of their being based on) the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are like illusory things and so forth.

This summarizes the grasping at the duality of internal and external phenomena. "Phenomena external to one's own mind" refers to the essential nature of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
"Aggregates within one's own mind" refers to the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the images that arise as transformations of one's own mind.
Regarding "either existent or non-existent": the objective parts of the images are existent, whereas the falsely conceptualized provisional phenomena are non-existent. Furthermore, the seventh...
The former exists, while the sixth does not. Regarding the statement that "all exist":
this is because the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) that arises as a transformation upon the sixth consciousness must necessarily exist, as has already been clarified previously.

Nevertheless, although it is admitted that all such image-aspects resembling phenomena arise as transformations upon this mind, they exist merely like an illusion because they are of the nature of the dependent-origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*). If [the object]...
To grasp at things as being substantially existent is *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). Like the daughter of a barren woman or the horns of a rabbit, they are definitively non-existent.

Having established these two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he further cites the sacred teachings (*āgama*) to conclude the proof. As the *Śata-śāstra* states: "All that is perceived is the activity of consciousness;
apart from consciousness, there is not a single phenomenon that is real. Due to the repeated habituation to various views since beginningless time," [it appears thus].

What is habitually perceived arises appearing as various phenomenal characteristics (dharma-nimitta) according to encountered conditions and according to the specific maturation of one's own seeds, just like things seen in a dream;
all are falsely manifested and not a single one is real. All are produced by the mind of consciousness (vijñāna-citta).
[Objection: If that is so, then the Mahāyāna must be like a dream or the speech of a mute, for it negates—
All phenomena are entirely empty; they cannot be explained as having distinct natures, whether mundane or supramundane.

How great is this suffering! We cannot rejoice in such illusory dharmas and meanings established by this Mahāyāna, for all phenomena can be directly perceived; it is impossible to deny what is directly perceived.
Because of the nature of phenomena, [the Buddha] replied: "How extraordinary and pitiable! These foolish people of meager merit cannot believe in or understand the meaning of the Mahāyāna teachings.
If there were one who could see, there would be a seer and something seen; yet since the seer does not exist, who is it that sees the object seen?
Because all things that see cannot examine themselves to know that they possess an intrinsic nature, nor can they examine others—at the time of such investigation, the seer..."
That which is perceived is entirely non-existent. Therefore, one should not cling to the idea that presently perceived phenomena possess a determinate intrinsic nature.
This is because, when the mind turns back [upon itself], all objects of perception are merely false and illusory. Why is this so? Because at the time of recollection...

In reality, there are no various objective realms such as seeing and so forth; rather, they arise as various appearances resembling seeing and other such objects through the transformation of one's own mind according to causes and conditions.
Because that which is recollected is not real, there is only the arising of what is called a false recollection.

It is named "recollection" (*smṛti*) because it is the turning back of the mind to pursue and remember the essential characteristics of dharmas previously experienced. One should recollect [them] in this way.
At the time of recollecting, since the objects previously experienced do not exist, the one who recollects likewise does not exist.
That which is called "recollection" is a conventional designation established in accordance with habitual tendencies and inverted views.

Due to this recollection, sentient beings in the world falsely give rise to various conceptualizations and disputes, vying to grasp at the self-nature and distinctions of phenomena, and thus sink into evil views.
Mud. Unable to emerge on its own. If there were nothing seen and nothing heard, then everything would be utterly non-existent.
How is it that at this time one weaves stones into a raft? This concludes the two preceding refutations of the clinging to dharmas.

Thus, because the mind is agitated and turbid by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) grasped by non-Buddhists and those of other vehicles, it appears as those [external objects] and evolves accordingly.

This is the third summary: since the self (*ātman*) and dharmas apart from consciousness do not exist as real entities, it is certain that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) do not take form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*), dissociated dharmas (*viprayukta-dharma*), or unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)—which are separate from consciousness—as their objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Because they are separate...

Because there are no substantial entities external to consciousness, the direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*) must necessarily depend upon truly existent dharmas that possess substance.
If forms and other phenomena were not transformations of mind, they could never be directly perceived. The following two syllogisms [are presented] below.

"Present" distinguishes [the present] from the past and future. Regarding the conditions for contact in the present, there must necessarily be a simultaneous arising of a single aggregate (*skandha*) of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) in mutual association; therefore, it is called an "aggregate.

Since each of the eight consciousnesses possesses four parts, its own seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) can only directly perceive its own object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), and cannot directly perceive the four parts of other consciousnesses; hence, it is said to be "present."
Regarding the mind and mental factors within that particular collection, they are not the direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the consciousness within this collection.

The reason is that they are subsumed under a different collection; they are like that which is not an object, such as form, which is not the object of auditory consciousness, or sound, which is not the object of visual consciousness.

That is to say, within a single consciousness, the mental factors (caitta) that coexist in the same aggregate do not directly perceive the mind-king (citta) with which they coexist, because the substance of the king and the factors are distinct.

This is analogous to other things that are not objects of perception. "The object of perception" refers to the image-part (nimittabhāga), while "the perceiver" refers to the seeing-part (darśanabhāga).
"Other things that are not objects of perception" means that those which do not face the perceiver are designated as "other. For this reason...

Second, the meaning of inference (*anumāna*). It can be seen that external objects (*bāhyārtha*) are entirely non-existent; there are only internal consciousnesses (*vijñapti*) arising as if they were external objects.
Furthermore, this is proven by citing a sūtra.
An objection is raised: "If there are no objects apart from consciousness, how can it be said that the mind evolves as if appearing as external objects?"
The fourth section provides a further explanation of the external objection. This objection arises from the word "resembling" (*sādṛśya*) mentioned above. Specifically, it asks:

regarding the statement that the perceived aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is said to resemble the self and dharmas, to what does it resemble? The answer is: it is said to be "resembling" in the sense that the internal resembles the external, and existence resembles non-existence;

it is on this basis that "resemblance" is predicated. Therefore, the objection states: for there to be a thing resembling something, there must first be a real thing (*bhūtārtha*); based upon these two things, [the resemblance is established].

Only after [the existence of] common characteristics can one speak of a thing that resembles [it] as being "provisional. Just as when there is a real fire, one then speaks of a person who resembles fire;
because this person possesses the qualities of fierce redness resembling fire, one may then provisionally designate this person as "fire."
Since my dharmas do not exist, to what could they possibly resemble? How could cow-hair possibly resemble tortoise-hair?
Since resemblance is not established, how can you say that the mind transforms by resembling them?

That objection is irrational because it [seeks to] separate the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) from consciousness; thus, these conventional designations (*prajñapti*) are not established based on a reality. This explanation of the objection is divided into two parts:

first, the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*); second, the application to the principle (*dārṣṭāntika*). Within the illustration, there is both a general and a specific analysis. In the general analysis, the two characters "true fire" (*tattvāgni*) are specifically refuted, because they use "true fire" as an analogy for the self and phenomena they grasp.

You say: [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on a Buddhist philosophical treatise (likely related to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* or similar Yogācāra works), discussing the critique of a non-Buddhist opponent who posits a real self and phenomena distinct from consciousness.*

Regarding the true fire, since it has already been refuted as being non-existent, why labor to raise the point again? This is because, as previously demonstrated in detail, the grasping at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) is entirely untenable.
Therefore, whether one speaks metaphorically based on a "class" (*jāti*) or based on a "substance" (*dravya*), the so-called "fire" and so forth are all unestablished.

That which shares common attributes is called a "class"; that which possesses a common essence is called a "substance. To rely on a class is to rely on a shared property; to rely on a substance is to rely on the true fire. [The following section] divides...
The second section refutes this. Regarding the refutation of the category of "homogeneity" (*sabhāga*): Fire has the qualities of being hot and illuminating as its defining characteristics.
Since the human body lacks these qualities despite having a fierce and red appearance, it is not of the same class.

If one could metaphorically designate a human being as "fire" even though it shares no common quality with fire, then one might likewise metaphorically apply names such as "fire" to water and other substances. Why would this not be the case?

This is analogous to the case of categories. If you claim that although their qualities differ, the person and the "fierce red" (the marks of a rākṣasa) are always inseparable and may thus be metaphorically identified, then we observe that the fierce red is not the person, and the person is not the fierce red.
Furthermore, even when the fierce red resides within the person, there are times when it does not manifest. How, then, can they be said to be inseparable? Since they do not coexist...
Furthermore, they are mutually distinct. If one could only employ a metaphorical designation based on a similarity between categories, then one should not say that there is a "person resembling fire.
Yet, it is commonly said that there is a person resembling fire; thus, we know that metaphorical designations are not established based on a resemblance to a real entity.

To refute the claim that [the designation] relies on a real entity: for a person and fire to share a single substance, only then could one say the designation relies on a real entity. [But] the person and the fire's intensity...
The quality of redness does not exist as a common substance; therefore, the principle of designating it based on a real entity is also untenable.
That is to say, the quality of intense redness produces heat and light when present in fire, whereas it causes bodily heat and mental distress in a person; thus, their natures are distinct.
Furthermore, as for their bases, sentient and insentient entities are each distinct; thus, there is no common quality upon which to base a metaphorical designation.

To do so would entail the fallacy of conflating water with fire, just as in the previous case. If it is argued that because humans possess the quality of warmth (*ūṣman*), they can be metaphorically designated as "fire," this is also logically untenable.
To say that fire exists within a person refers to its characteristics of intensity and redness, not [to mere warmth].
In the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, it is said that a person is like fire; thus we know that even metaphorical designations (*prajñapti*) do not necessarily rely upon real entities (*dravya*).
Furthermore, if a metaphor must rely on a real entity to be established, [it follows that] one metaphorically designates "self" and "dharmas" with respect to what is transformed by consciousness.
This further clarifies that conventional phenomena are not established based upon ultimate phenomena. The subsequent conclusion establishes the correct principle. The *Zongjing* says:

"Why are they called 'specific characteristics' (*svalakṣaṇa*) and 'common characteristics' (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)? It is said: If the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon is known only by realized wisdom (*pratyātmajñāna*), it is beyond the reach of verbal expression."

This is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). If a phenomenon’s essential nature is accessible through verbal expression and is the object of conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*), this is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding "conceptual cognition," it refers to the mind that engages in mental construction and interpretation; this is called conceptual cognition.

Regarding "that which expresses" (*vācaka*), the names, phrases, and phonemes within the interpreting mind, as well as the names, phrases, and phonemes within sound, are the expressers; none of them attain the expressed (*vācya*).
This refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). It shows that the conventional does not rely on the real; it functions solely based on the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding this very reality, the actual substance of mind and consciousness is not called "real. Rather, it is the self-nature of the phenomena apprehended by the mind, which is beyond the reach of verbal expression and cannot be grasped by conceptual cognition (*kalpanā*), that is termed "real.
This is known only by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) wisdom; its nature is free from verbal expression and—
This wisdom-discrimination emerges from the true essence; it is not something that can be reached by intellectual designations.
Unlike the nature of form and other phenomena, its nature is like that of water’s moisture—it can only be realized through direct experience and is beyond the reach of verbal expression.

Following upon the five sensory consciousnesses, the sixth mental consciousness arises and, by taking this wisdom as its object, produces speech and so forth; these are merely the commonality between the object of cognition and the dharma expressed.

It is a characteristic, not its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, by negating the attainment of its own specific characteristic, one is said to attain the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

If, among those transformed [phenomena], there were a common characteristic that could be attained, then it would be the attainment of a substantial entity (*svabhāva*); consequently, all phenomena would be expressible and cognizable.

Therefore, it is said that even common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) are not reached by cognition, yet this is not because they are grasped as substantial entities, for they are not firmly apprehended.
Furthermore, if verbal expression were to adhere to intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), then when the word "fire" is spoken, fire should burn the mouth;
for fire has the nature of burning things as its intrinsic characteristic. Cognition is likewise: when fire is cognized, fire should burn the mind. Yet, in reality, it does not burn the mind.
And it does not burn the mouth. This clarifies that both the conditions and the verbal expression obtain the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

If this were so, why would calling out "fire" not result in obtaining water? [One might argue: "Because one does not obtain the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire, just as when calling out 'water'.

This reasoning is not correct, because there has been habitual practice of such common usage since beginningless time. Furthermore, the specific characteristic is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena; for example, fire is characterized by heat.
It is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). When one calls out "fire," because heat is not obtained, it cannot be the specific characteristic.

This heat is the specific characteristic because it is realized through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of tactile consciousness alone; it is not something obtained by means of names. As for the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), this refers to the meaning expressed by a name as the general characteristic.
For example, when expressing phenomena such as fire, that which excludes what is not fire and so forth is the meaning [of the term]. This meaning is...

Because it pervades all instances of fire, it is called the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). The signifier (*vācaka*) is speech; the signified (*vācya*) is conventional cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*).

This conventional cognition as a signifier also does not exist apart from this common characteristic, nor is there any other means (*upāya*) outside of it that establishes a "particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its basis.
Nevertheless, conventional cognition as a signifier necessarily arises based on similar vocal sounds. [Sound...]

Furthermore, when one abides in this conventional cognition that expresses [reality], one no longer undergoes cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). This is because both the expressive term and the expressed object cannot directly realize their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Thus, we know that conventional designations do not rely on real entities, but rather function by relying on "semblances" (*pratibimba*). A "semblance" refers to what is superimposed (*samāropa*);
that is to say, after a direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*) has cognized a specific characteristic, there subsequently arises a similar cognition at a later moment.
This is a reflected image manifested through conceptual differentiation; because one superimposes characteristics upon the basis of characteristics, it is called "semblance.
It is like a person looking into a mirror: the form and the reflection appear as two distinct individuals—is this not a case of superimposition?

Sound relies on cognition for its expression, functioning solely by depending on the superimposed semblance of characteristics; therefore, one cannot say that the conventional must necessarily rely on the ultimate reality.
Question: Since these provisional [entities] do not arise based upon the ultimate truth, upon what do these provisional self and dharmas depend for their arising? Answer:
Although they do not depend upon the ultimate truth, they exist by virtue of being manifested through the transformation of internal consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because those non-Buddhists and followers of other vehicles falsely imagine that there is a real self and dharmas external to the mind, this teaching of "internal" [self and dharmas] is spoken in order to refute and dispel such attachments. It refers to that which resembles a self and resembles dharmas.
"Transformed by consciousness. Its meaning is as follows: although external objects do not exist, from the perspective of your own grasping mind, they appear as if they truly exist;
therefore, they are merely "similar to" [external objects]. This refers to the internal appearing as the external, and the existent appearing as the non-existent.

This section concludes the present passage; more distantly, it concludes the previous verse which states: "By means of conventional designations of self and phenomena, there are various characteristics."

[The section on] "Transformation" concludes the first part: the explanation of the first three lines of the verse within the general exposition of the "Division on Consciousness-Only," based on the three phrases concerning what is transformed by consciousness.
Although the aspects transformed by consciousness are of infinite kinds, [the term] "maturation" (*vipāka*) refers only to those [aspects] mentioned here and not to all of them.

The second [section] explains the three types of transformational consciousness (*trividha-pariṇāma*). This refers to the latter three lines of the verse. This specifically explains the line in the verse:

"This transformational consciousness is only threefold. The phrase "the images transformed by consciousness" (*vijñāna-pariṇata-nimitta*) reiterates the wording from the preceding verse to encompass the various images of the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*).

Regarding why the first transformational consciousness is named *vipāka* (maturation): it is because there are three meanings. Namely, it matures through transformation; it is different [from its cause]; and...
It ripens at different times; it ripens from heterogeneous classes; because the fruit only ripens when the seed has undergone transformation.

Since the cause that produces the fruit and the ripening of that fruit are fixed as occurring at different times, and since the nature of the cause—whether wholesome or unwholesome—differs from the nature of the fruit, which is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*), they are distinct.

Thus, the character *yi* (different) pertains to the cause, and the character *shu* (ripening) pertains to the fruit. Because the cause and effect are not identical, they are analyzed as a *vyadhikaraṇa-karmadhāraya* compound: "the different [cause] and the ripening [fruit]. Alternatively, [it may be interpreted as...]

"Differentiation" (viśeṣa) refers to maturation (vipāka). If the term "differentiation" belongs to the fruit, then differentiation is itself maturation; alternatively, if "differentiation-maturation" (vipāka-viśeṣa) belongs to the present, then differentiation-maturation is consciousness itself—this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).
If "differentiation-maturation" belongs to the seed, then it is the "consciousness of differentiation-maturation"—this is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound).

Although the sixth consciousness also possesses maturation (*vipāka*), it constitutes only a single portion; since the eight consciousnesses possess maturation predominantly, they are said to have "predominantly maturational nature.
Regarding the second transformation, which is called "cognition and deliberation" (*manana*): "cognition" (*manas*) refers to thinking, and "deliberation" (*nāna*) refers to measuring.

It takes the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its internal self. "Constantly" (*nitya*) means uninterrupted; "thoroughly" (*parīkṣaka*) means grasping at a self. This is "cognition."

"Measurement" (*māna*) is "cognition" (*vijñāna*). This is an *appositional compound* (*karmadhāraya*). Although all cognitions possess the quality of deliberation (*manana*), some are constant but not discerning, while others are discerning but not constant.

Only the seventh [consciousness] is both constant and discerning; therefore, it alone is designated as such. Regarding the statement that the three transformative consciousnesses are called "those that cognize objects":

"cognize" (*liao*) means to fully comprehend (*parijñā*). Although the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are also capable of cognizing objects, they function by way of an internal orientation (*antarmukha-pravṛtti*). Only...
Because the sixth consciousness alone dwells in the external gate when cognizing subtle objects, it cognizes coarse phenomenal objects.
The word "and" (ca) clarifies that the term "and" in the verse indicates that the first five consciousnesses and the sixth consciousness combine to form a single type [of transformation].

This is because the first five consciousnesses must necessarily have a simultaneous mental consciousness arise when they apprehend objects. Next, the meaning of "transformative capacity" (pariṇāma) is explained: first, the transformative capacity as cause (hetu-pariṇāma), which is...
The Section on the Manifestation of Seeds: Seeds give rise to manifest activity; this is termed "causal habit-energy" (*hetuvāsanā*).
Within this, there are two parts: first the heading, and second the explanation. Regarding "habit-energy of equal outflow" (*niṣyandavāsanā*):

this refers to the seeds of the three natures within the [first] seven consciousnesses, each producing its own manifestation and perfuming the seeds of the eighth consciousness, thereby causing them to increase. This excludes only the eighth consciousness itself, as it cannot be perfumed. Differentiation...

Regarding "matured habitual tendencies": through the active manifestation of wholesome and unwholesome states within the first six consciousnesses, they perfume the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome maturation within the eighth consciousness, causing them to increase.
This excludes only the seventh consciousness, because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and is not a cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*).

The former is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); this is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Regarding the "resultant transformation" (*phala-pariṇāma*): it refers to the manifest results produced by the two aforementioned causes.
That is to say, those conditioned phenomena that are capable of manifesting transformation are termed "resultant transformation. As for the "various characteristics":

these refer to the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and subject-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mental concomitants associated with the eighth consciousness, as well as various manifest results such as suffering and pleasure.
Regarding the phrase "with the outflowing habitual tendencies as the causal condition," the following is a detailed explanation.

The first seven consciousnesses, through the power of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), perfume the eighth consciousness to form seeds that grow. Thus, the seeds of the three natures within the eight consciousnesses each produce their own manifestations;
these are called "outflowing fruits" (*niṣyandaphala*). Because the nature of the produced fruit is identical to that of the producing seed, cause and effect are similar.

They are called "outflows" (*niṣyanda*) because they belong to that same category: wholesome seeds produce wholesome manifest activities, afflictive seeds produce unwholesome manifest activities, and indeterminate seeds produce indeterminate manifest activities; these are the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*).

Obtaining a retribution of short life for killing and a retribution of long life for releasing living beings is called a "nominal outflow," which is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*). As for the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*):

With the preceding six types of wholesome and unwholesome karma acting as the preeminent dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), they induce the eighth consciousness as the retribution for the projective karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) performed toward others.

Because it continues uninterrupted over a long period of time, it is designated by the name "maturation" (*vipāka*). "Projecting" (*ākṣepa*) means "to draw forth. This refers to the power of karma to draw forth the collective retribution;
that is, when the first six consciousnesses perform wholesome or unwholesome karma, they project the eighth consciousness to undergo wholesome or unwholesome retribution. Such is its characteristic.

That which continues without interruption is called the *vipāka-phala* (maturation fruit). The karma produced by the first six consciousnesses, which can fulfill the two fruits of good and evil within their own respective consciousnesses, is called *vipākaja* (born of maturation).
Because it arises from the substance of the eighth [consciousness], it is not itself termed "maturation" (*vipāka*).
This is because the first six consciousnesses are intermittent and do not pervade the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) and so forth, nor exist during the state of no-mind (*acittaka*).

Because the six consciousnesses do not function during states such as meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the eighth consciousness is called the "master of total retribution" (*sāmānyavipākādhipati*), whereas the sixth is called the "master of individual retribution" (*viśeṣavipākādhipati*).

If one speaks only of "ripening" (*vipāka*) without qualification, it does not include individual retribution; however, by saying "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*), both the general and the individual are encompassed.

Because its causes are both wholesome and unwholesome while its fruit is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*), it is said that "the fruit differs from the cause. This is the meaning of the term "ripening" (*vipāka*).

Although there are many meanings [to this term], here we take only that which undergoes perfuming, maintains seeds, and is the transformative consciousness (*pariṇāma*)—the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) that is the fruit of both good and evil—as "ripening" (*vipāka*).
This does not refer to all other meanings, such as transformation at a different time or by different noble ones (*ārya*).
This concludes the brief discussion above on *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only).

The detailed exposition of the section on Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) below is divided into two parts: first, the elucidation of the three types of transformative consciousness; second, the response to the five external inquiries.
The first part is further divided into three sections, namely the first two of the three types of transformative consciousness.

Now, the first transformation is divided into three parts: first, the conclusion of the preceding section and the presentation of the question; second, Vasubandhu’s verse; third, the explanation of the verse’s meaning.
Although the three names of the transformations have already been briefly explained, what are the characteristics of the first transformation?
First, the preceding summary and inquiry.
The verse states: "The initial ālayavijñāna... constantly evolving like a violent torrent; it is abandoned at the stage of the arhat.
This constitutes the second half of the second verse, along with the third and fourth verses, totaling twelve sections. First.

1. The gate of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*): namely, the initial ālayavijñāna. 2. The gate of the characteristic of the fruit (*phalalakṣaṇa*): namely, maturation (*vipāka*). 3. The gate of the characteristic of the cause (*hetulakṣaṇa*):

namely, all seeds (*sarvabīja*). 4. The gate of the unknowable (*anirjñeya*): namely, that which is unknowable. 5. The gate of the object-condition (*ālambana*): namely, appropriation and the locus (*upādāna-sthāna*).

6. The gate of the aspect (*ākāra*): namely, discernment (*vijñapti*). 7. The gate of association (*samprayoga*): namely, its constant association with contact (*sparśa*) and attention (*manasikāra*).
1. The gate of association with feeling, perception, and volition; 2. The gate of the eight factors associated with feeling, which is exclusively the feeling of equanimity;
3. The gate of the three natures, which is the non-obscured neutral; 4. The gate of mental factors following the example of the king, wherein contact and the others are likewise;
5. The gate of cause, effect, dharma, and analogy, wherein it perpetually flows like a torrent; 6. The gate of the stages of subduing and abandoning, namely the [stage of] *ā*...
The state of Arhatship abandons [the afflictions].
Regarding the explanation of the meaning of the verse for the [remaining] three lower stages, there are two parts:
first, the direct explanation of the verse’s meaning; second, the proof that the substance of consciousness exists.
First, the correct explanation of the meaning of the verse is divided into eight parts.

The treatise states: Regarding the first transformative consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), because its faults are more serious than those of the *ālaya* mentioned in the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, it is specifically explained here.
First, the explanation of the gate of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). In the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, it is called *ālayavijñāna*.

Paramārtha translated this name as "the non-perishing consciousness" (*wumoshishi*), taking the sense of not losing [what has been grasped]. Master Xuanzang translated it according to its meaning as "the storehouse consciousness" (*zangshi*), because it can contain and store the seeds of all phenomena.

Thus, the essence of this consciousness possesses the threefold meaning of "storehouse": it is the store where [seeds] are stored (*neng-cang*), that which is stored within it (*suo-cang*), and that which is clung to as a store (*zhi-cang*).
First, "that which can store" (ālaya) has the meaning of being able to contain and store. It is like a treasury, which is able to contain and store precious gems; thus it receives the name "store.
Because this [consciousness] is able to contain and store the seeds of defilement (*saṃkleśa*), it is called the "store" (*ālaya*).

It also carries the meaning of "sustaining. This is explained from the perspective of sustaining the seeds. Second, "that which is stored" has the meaning of being the basis (*āśraya*). It is like a treasury, which is...

Because it is the basis for the jewels and so forth, and because this consciousness is the locus of the defilements (*saṃkleśa*), it is described here from the perspective of receiving perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Regarding the three aspects of being "appropriated" (*ālaya*): it means to hold firmly and not relinquish, just as a storehouse of gold, silver, and so forth is firmly guarded by people.
Because it is grasped as one's own internal self, it is called a "store" (*ālaya*). This consciousness is firmly grasped as such by the defiled *manas*.

Therefore, it is called a "storehouse" (*ālaya*). The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* (*Qixin lun chao*) explains that regarding the eighth consciousness’s meaning of being both the "capable store" (*neng-cang*) and the "stored-in" (*suo-cang*):
first, as for the meaning of being "stored-in," it means that the substance of this consciousness is the locus where the sense-faculties, the body, the seeds, and the receptacle world are stored.

This is because the sense-faculties, the body, and so forth are the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of this consciousness, just like objects and images within a storehouse, or as the body [is contained] within...
Within the chamber, if one seeks the ālayavijñāna, it resides solely within form and mind; if one seeks the maṇi jewel, it resides solely within the blue and yellow.
Next is the meaning of "concealing": this refers to how phenomena such as the sense organs and the body are all concealed within the body of consciousness.

Just as images appear within a pearl, so too when one seeks all phenomena, they are found entirely within the *ālayavijñāna*; when one seeks all images, they are found entirely within the *maṇi* jewel.
These two meanings function respectively as the subject and the object. As for "defiled" (*saṃkleśa*), this distinguishes it from pure phenomena.
When they act as mutual conditions, they constitute mutual cause and effect; this will be explained in the subsequent section, wherein both the subject and the object are fully present.
