This is established.
Furthermore, that same sutra states: "[... it is not the case that the various evolving consciousnesses possess such a meaning.
This refers to the second verse of the aforementioned sutra; its first three lines reveal that the eighth consciousness contains the seeds of all phenomena (*dharmas*).

My son, it receives the name *ālaya*. The fourth phrase reveals that this is taught for those of the Bodhisattva vehicle; only upon attaining the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*) is one called a "Victorious One" (*jin*).
Because the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of the eighth consciousness is able to maintain the seeds, it is called the "seed-consciousness."
Because it is able to contain and store all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), it is called the *ālaya*.

This eighth consciousness is not like the Sāṃkhya doctrine of the *pradhāna* (primordial nature) transforming into the *mahat* and so forth, wherein the characteristics transform while the essence remains one, or the fruit arises and ceases while the cause remains eternally one.
The *ālayavijñāna* contains the seeds of phenomena; from these seeds, [phenomena] arise.
Manifestation arises from seeds; the two entities of cause and effect are not identical, because the seeds belong to the eighth consciousness while the manifest activities belong to the first seven.

Therefore, the dharmas that depend [upon consciousness] and the consciousness which serves as their support arise and perish together, yet they are not different, because the cause perishes as the fruit arises, and the fruit arises as the cause perishes. Thus, this refutes the false attachment to difference and clearly reveals the correct [view].

Regarding the principle [of the *ālayavijñāna*], the explanation based on the Three Piṭakas is found in the lower section of the *Miśraka*. The interpretation is as seen in the preceding text. "Having already entered," etc., next explains the fourth birth;
because it is immediately bound to that [birth], it is like a lodestone attracting iron.
The two drops of the parents' semen and blood are like the iron; the eighth consciousness is like the lodestone. In a single kṣaṇa, it grasps and dwells [in them] simultaneously.
The seeds of the sense faculties, objects, and so forth, also arise as manifest activity from within their own consciousness; this is called "grasping for rebirth.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "As for the power of continuity, there are nine types of death-minds that are associated with self-love (*ātmabhāvātṛṣṇā*), which cause the continuity of birth in the desire, form, and formless realms respectively within the three realms. That is to say, from the desire realm..."
When passing away from there and being reborn in the desire realm, one links the continuity of rebirth with a death-consciousness associated with self-love (*kāmarāga*) belonging to the desire realm.
If one is reborn in the form or formless realms, one links the continuity of rebirth with a death-consciousness associated with self-love belonging to the form or formless realms.
Thus, when passing away from the form or formless realms, if one...
Whether one is born there or born in another place, one should know that there are six types of mind, as appropriate to each case.

Furthermore, this craving for one's own self-existence (*ātmabhāvātṛṣṇā*) is exclusively innate (*sahaja*), does not clearly discern its object, and is comprised within the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature;
yet it is capable of differentiating the various states of one's own self-existence. By the power of this [craving], ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*)...

Now, this craving arises in active manifestation within the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the Avīci hell, and likewise for noble ones (*ārya*) who have not yet abandoned desire.
At the time of death, up until the stage of unclear perception is reached, this craving can arise; however, it is discerned and suppressed by the power of its antidote.
For noble ones who have already abandoned desire, the power of the antidote is so strong that [such craving does not arise].
Although it has not been permanently severed, this craving no longer manifests; rather, it causes [the existence] to arise and continue through the power of its latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

At the very first moment of the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is exclusively non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), because it is comprised within the category of maturation (*vipāka*).
From that point onward, it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, as the case may be, with the exception of that [craving].
The mind of death (*cyuti-citta*). Because the mind of death within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is always defiled, it is like the mind of death at the end of existence (*maraṇa-bhava*).
The momentary mind that links the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) is likewise exclusively unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

However, in the case of Bodhisattvas who take rebirth through the power of their vows (*praṇidhāna*), one should know that all their minds at the time of death and so forth are invariably wholesome (*kuśala*). Because they maintain these three meanings, it is called [the "mind of death"].

Regarding the phrase "one who has attained true realization" (*tattvābhisamaya*): there are six types of realization, namely: realization through reflection (*cintā*), realization through faith (*śraddhā*), realization through ethical discipline (*śīla*), realization through the knowledge of the truths (*jñāna-satyābhisamaya*), realization through the knowledge of the limits [of existence] (*koṭi-jñāna-satyābhisamaya*), and ultimate realization (*niṣṭhābhisamaya*).
That which occurs prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is called "semblance," while that which occurs upon the stages is called "true.

This refers precisely to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) arising after the Bodhisattva’s path of vision (*darśana-mārga*). Having attained this wisdom, one is able to realize and comprehend the *ālayavijñāna*.
Only then is one called a "Victor" (*jin*). The Blessed One specifically taught this consciousness for their sake.

Alternatively, those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) may also be called "Victors," because within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), they have already been able to believe in and understand the nature and characteristics of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), and have generated the most supreme and intense aspiration, seeking the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*);
for them as well, the Blessed One has taught it. It is not that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and so forth possess such [qualities].
This meaning is summarized in the verse, which explains that only the eighth [consciousness] possesses such characteristics.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* also states this, saying: "Only the eighth consciousness has such characteristics."
This is the third verse from the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. Regarding "ādāna," this is translated here as "appropriation" (or "grasping").
There are three types of appropriation: first, appropriating the seeds of all phenomena so that they are not lost;

second, appropriating the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) and their bases (i.e., the body and the *māṃsendriya*, or "dust-like" sense organs) so that they do not decay; and third, appropriating the continuity of rebirth, which refers to [the state of] existence.

Regarding the "body within the intermediate state" (*antarābhava*) at the final stage, when the eighth consciousness first undergoes rebirth, it possesses the meaning of grasping (*upādāna*), linking birth, and continuity.
"Linking" (*saṃdhi*) means binding and belonging. Within the mother’s womb, in that single moment of receiving this consciousness, it is termed the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
To say it is "without intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*) means not believing that the eighth consciousness constitutes the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena.
Therefore, if the eighth consciousness did not exist, there would be no Buddha-nature; thus, they are called icchantikas who lack nature.

The non-Buddhist outsiders of the Western Heavens, because they do not believe that this consciousness is the foundation of all dharmas, either cling to the principle of primordial darkness (prakṛti) or cling to the principle of Great Existence (mahāsattā).
Some cling to the nature of permanence, while others cling to the nature of annihilation;

thus they are tossed about and prevented from attaining liberation, and for this reason, they cannot fathom its depths—it is therefore called "profound. Śrāvakas who seek only tranquility do not comprehend its characteristics;

they reckon the six consciousnesses and the three poisons as the root of all phenomena, and because they are submerged by these, they remain unaware of it and thus fail to attain thorough penetration. Therefore...
It is said: "Extremely subtle. This explains the second phrase, "the true seed of all phenomena," which follows below.
Regarding the phrase "arising when struck by conditions," it refers to how visual consciousness arises through nine conditions, and so forth. As the Sūtra says:

"O Viśālamati, because the ādāna-vijñāna serves as their support and basis, the six groups of consciousness arise—namely, visual consciousness, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness. This...

Therein, consciousness exists. With the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; simultaneously with that eye-consciousness, there occurs the functioning of a conceptual mental consciousness that accompanies it, being simultaneous and having the same object.
Therein, consciousness exists; with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles as conditions, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness arise;
simultaneously with those ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses, there occurs [the functioning of a conceptual mental consciousness] that accompanies them, being simultaneous...
"Vast Intelligence, when a conceptualizing mental consciousness operates with the same objective field [as the sensory consciousness], if at that time a single visual consciousness operates,
then at that very moment there is only one conceptualizing mental consciousness operating with the same range of activity as the visual consciousness.
If at that time two, three, four, or five groups of consciousnesses operate, then at that very moment there is only one conceptualizing [mental consciousness]."
The mental consciousness and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses function with the same objective domain. O Broad Wisdom, it is like a great torrential flow of water:
if the conditions for the arising of a single wave appear, only one wave arises; if the conditions for the arising of two or many waves appear, many waves arise.
Nevertheless, this torrential water flows as its own kind, constantly, without interruption or exhaustion. Furthermore, like...
Just as when conditions for the arising of a single reflection appear before a well-purified mirror surface, only one reflection arises;
and when conditions for the arising of two or many reflections appear, many reflections arise— yet this mirror surface does not transform into those reflections,
nor is there any depletion or exhaustion to be found therein— so too, O Vast Intelligence, by means of the ādāna-vijñāna which is like a violent torrent...

For the sake of providing a basis and for the sake of establishment: if at that time the conditions for the arising of a single visual consciousness are present, then at that very moment a single visual consciousness arises;
if at that time the conditions for the arising of up to five groups of consciousness are present, then at that very moment five groups of consciousness arise.
From the words "All [consciousnesses] are without intrinsic nature" onwards, the latter two [points] are explained.
Regarding these verses: they are spoken by the superior ones to the ignorant. As An-hui (Asvabhāva) says:

"Those who harbor the view of self are not shown [this teaching], for fear that they will conceptually construct and cling to it as a self. How could such a class of people distinguish between one category and another?
Because their mode of conceptual construction and clinging remains uniform and unchanging throughout the limits of birth and death, only the eighth consciousness possesses [this nature]."
Such are the characteristics. In summary, the intent of this verse explains only the eight consciousnesses.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also states this (up to): "It is included within the authority of the *Ekottarika-āgama* and other such scriptures."
Fourth, this introduces a verse from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which restates the preceding meaning: "The eighth [consciousness] is like the ocean;
the winds of external objects stir the ocean of the mind, constantly giving rise to the waves of various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

Thus, while the characteristics of the waves are intermittent, the seawater is always continuous; while the evolving consciousnesses are intermittent, the eighth consciousness is eternally continuous. Therefore, one should know [this]."

There exists something like the ocean-like storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Because the visual and other sensory consciousnesses are subject to transformation, interruption, and discontinuity, they cannot serve as the support for all cognitions;
they lack the quality of the great ocean, which constantly flows in succession and gives rise to waves of cognition.

This has been extensively revealed in these immeasurable Mahāyāna sūtras, appearing scattered throughout the various teachings of the Noble Ones (*āptāgama*). How could it be limited to what was mentioned previously?
The numerous verses cited here and the various Mahāyāna sūtras all accord with selflessness (*anātman*) and oppose the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).
They avoid cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and incline toward its cessation (*nivṛtti*). They praise the Three Jewels (*triratna*) and censure non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

They manifest the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), while refuting the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*) and the six categories (*ṣat-padārtha*) and so forth. This is the Mahāyāna Dharma; its principle is without error.
[This is] inverted. It is only those who delight in the Mahāyāna that are permitted to be shown [this teaching].

Not only in the Mahāyāna, but even within the Śrāvaka schools, sūtras such as the *Ekottarika-āgama* are all subsumed under the authority of the Buddha’s authentic word (*āptāgama*). Furthermore, the secret teachings refer to this by the name *ālayavijñāna*, as will be seen in detail below.
Because the Śrāvakas do not believe in the existence of the *ālayavijñāna*, it was thus taught through indirect guidance. This is established.

The *Pramāṇa* states: "All Mahāyāna sūtras are subsumed under the category of authoritative scripture (*āptāgama-pramāṇa*), because they are included within the category of *sūtra*, just like the *Aṅguttara-nikāya* and so forth.

Furthermore, the noble Maitreya established [their authority] through seven reasons, up to: 'because they possess different textual expressions that counteract [wrong views], their existence or non-existence is thus established.'"
The five reasons for citing Maitreya as the seventh cause: having already cited the present Śākyamuni, one further cites the future Maitreya to prove that the Mahāyāna was spoken by the Buddha.

First, regarding "that which was not previously predicted": this refers to those of the Hīnayāna who claim that the Mahāyāna sūtras were not spoken by the Buddha, asserting that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, other individuals [fabricated them] in order to destroy the true Dharma of the Hīnayāna.
While this Mahāyāna was being taught, Maitreya challenged it, asking: "Why did the World-Honored One not previously grant a prophecy regarding these terrifying matters?

The Buddha, within the sūtras, has stated that during the age of the final dharma (mofa), there will be various māra-kings who enter into my teaching, don my kashaya robes, and destroy my true dharma until the dharma is utterly extinguished. Regarding such matters as these, the Buddha previously—

Regarding the prophecy: if Mahāyāna sūtras were spoken by those who destroy the Dharma after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, why do they not differ from other [texts] in providing prior prophecies concerning terrifying events?

Second, regarding both being practiced together: since both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are intended for two types of capacities and have both been in circulation from the beginning, and since there are indeed two types of capacities, why is there only one vehicle (yāna)? Why do you allow that the Hīnayāna is the Buddha’s [teaching]?
Regarding what has been stated: first, the claim that the Mahāyāna alone is not the word of the Buddha;

second, the point that it is not the domain of others, meaning that the Mahāyāna teachings are known only by those of great capacity and wisdom, and are not within the sphere of other people; therefore, they were not taught for them, and even if taught, they would not believe.
Third, the point that it should be universally established (*prasiddha*): since the present Buddha and other Buddhas are one and the same Buddha, if one claims that the Mahā...

If one claims that this was spoken by other Buddhas and not by our current Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, then it is established beyond doubt that the Mahāyāna sūtras are indeed the word of the Buddha, leaving no room for dissent. Fifth, regarding "existence and non-existence":
if one accepts the existence of the Mahāyāna, one must believe that these sūtras are the word of the Buddha; apart from such sūtras, it is impossible to find a separate Mahāyāna.
Because it has been attained. If there were no Mahāyāna, there would likewise be no Hīnayāna. Why is this? Because apart from the Mahāyāna, there is no principle for attaining Buddhahood;
who, then, would appear in the world to teach the Great and Small Vehicles? Therefore, we maintain that the Hīnayāna is indeed the word of the Buddha.
This is not the teaching of the Mahāyāna; logically, it cannot be so. Regarding the six types of antidotes:

wisdom is twofold—namely, that which accords with reality (*yathārtha*) and that which accords with the full extent of phenomena (*yāvadbhāvikatā*), and the fundamental (*mūla*) and subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) [wisdoms], as well as the knowledge of all paths (*sarvamārgajñatā*).

Wisdom that accords with reality, fundamental wisdom, and the knowledge of all paths are non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Wisdom that accords with the full extent of phenomena, subsequently attained wisdom, and all [other forms] are conceptual wisdom (*savikalpa-jñāna*). Non-conceptual wisdom...
It does not rely on the mind, nor does it take external objects as its condition. It realizes that all phenomena are entirely suchness (*tathatā*).
Since object and wisdom are non-different, only those who diligently practice according to the Mahāyāna can induce this wisdom when it arises. At the moment it arises:

That one could truly counteract the root afflictions and secondary afflictions is not what was taught by the Buddha; who, then, could achieve this? Regarding the seven points where the meaning differs from the text:
the teachings of the Mahāyāna are profound and subtle in their principles; those who merely skim the surface of the text have not yet mastered its meaning.
They hastily give rise to slander, claiming that these are not the words of the Buddha; this is merely the fault of the ignorant.

There is a verse in the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Treatise on Ornamentation) that sets forth these seven meanings; it was previously unrecorded. "Prior non-recording" is the first cause, and "co-occurrence" is the second cause.

That it is not the objective sphere of others is the third reason. That it is universally established (*prasiddha*) is the fourth reason. That there is existence and non-existence is the fifth reason.
That it is an antidote (*pratipakṣa*) is the sixth reason. That the phrasing is different is the seventh reason.
In the sūtras of other schools as well, there are implicit teachings [extending up to] which definitively reveal only this *ālayavijñāna*.

Regarding the citation of the four schools of the Hīnayāna as being taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*): it was done so that they might not give rise to conceptual attachments; therefore, it was indicated cryptically rather than stated explicitly.

Now, the Master of the Treatise identifies these as all being this eighth consciousness. The Mahāsāṃghika school... [is... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)
The name *Āgama* refers to a section within the Sūtras of the Hīnayāna. This is the name of a sūtra belonging to the Mahāsāṃghika school.

This sūtra speaks of the "fundamental consciousness," which is precisely the eighth consciousness. It is called "fundamental" because the visual consciousness and the others arise in dependence upon this consciousness;
it is like how stems, branches, and leaves exist in dependence upon the root of a tree. It is not the mental consciousness that can serve as the basis for the visual consciousness.

The supports for consciousness and the other [mental factors] cannot function as faculties (*indriya*) because they are not constant. Furthermore, because [the faculties] produce stems and so forth, [the ālayavijñāna] is distinct.

Second, the Sthavira school asserts the existence of the *bhavāṅga-vijñāna* (life-continuum consciousness), which is precisely the eighth consciousness. The essence of this *bhavāṅga-vijñāna* is eternally uninterrupted and pervades the three realms of existence;
thus it is called "the three existences" (*tri-bhava*). The term "portion" (*aṅga*) has the meaning of "cause"; that is, it is the cause of the three existences.

All [these] arise from this consciousness. Within the Saṃmitīya school (Vibhajyavāda), it is taught that there exists the "aggregate that exhausts birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra-kṣaya-skandha*), which is precisely the eighth consciousness.

There are three types of aggregates: first, the "momentary aggregate," referring to phenomena that undergo arising and ceasing within a single instant; second, the "lifetime aggregate," referring to phenomena that persist and evolve continuously until death; and third, the "aggregate that exhausts birth-and-death."

This refers to the dharmas that persist until the attainment of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*). Because they take this eighth [consciousness] as their object and are constantly present throughout the nine stages of the three realms, wherever there is birth and death, they always and universally serve as its support.
They are only relinquished at the end of the Great Vehicle’s diamond-mind (*vajra-citta*), when all afflictions are exhausted;
therefore, they are called the "aggregates that exhaust birth and death" (*ātyantika-jāti-maraṇa-skandha*). This is because they consist of the aggregates of form and the formless realm. Not...

[If it were otherwise,] it would not extend throughout birth and death (*saṃsāra*), because feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*) cease [in the attainment of cessation]. Feeling and perception do not extend throughout birth and death.
Nor do the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) extend throughout birth and death, because they cannot be found apart from this [mind] and form (*rūpa*).

Thus, as for the aggregates that extend throughout birth and death, if one excludes the eighth [consciousness], what else could it be? The Sarvāstivādins say that this consciousness is named the *ālayavijñāna*. It is the object of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Delight (*nandi*), longing (*prīti*), joy (*muditā*), and the fourfold *ālaya*—these refer to the seventh manas-consciousness which craves that eighth [consciousness].

These four names are established based on its taking that [eighth consciousness] as its object in its general and specific aspects across the three periods of time. "Craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) is the general object; the other three are specific objects:
namely, delighting in the past self, longing for the present self, and rejoicing in the future self. This refers to this seventh [consciousness] and that eighth...
The eight types of sentient beings are thus; they mistake the conventional for the real, and in every thought-moment they are greedily attached to it as the locus of true love.
They will never grasp at the five aggregates as being truly beloved.

For those born in places of suffering, although they feel extreme revulsion toward their own aggregates, they have never abandoned the notion of a self; therefore, one knows that what is reviled resides within the aggregates. What...
Self is what I love. Even the five sensual pleasures are not the true object of attachment;
for one who has attained the first dhyāna does not love the five sensual pleasures, but loves self. Furthermore, pleasant feeling is not the true object of attachment;

for one who cultivates the four dhyānas and possesses meditative concentration (dhyāna) rejects exquisite pleasure as if discarding a mixture of poison, yet still loves self. Do not allow that pleasure to defile it.
Because it is defiled by the self, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is also not the locus of true attachment.

This means that from the first fruit up to the third fruit, although the afflictions of discrimination have been severed and the view of a self does not arise, because the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) have not yet been exhausted, one still clings to an internal self.

Furthermore, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are also not the locus of true attachment; this means that even for those who practice the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), although they loathe the first seven consciousnesses, they still cling to a self.
Therefore, the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is also not the locus of true attachment; for even though one does not love form within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one still loves the "self.
Furthermore, the dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) are also not the locus of true delight, because they lack substantial reality. Question:

We clearly observe that sentient beings are attached to the various aggregates (*skandha*) and take pleasure in the five objects of desire (*pañcakāmaguṇa*). Why are these not considered loci of attachment? Answer: This is based on...
The *ālayavijñāna* is the object of craving for the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth; it is not the object of craving for the aggregates themselves.

It is like a person who is attached to his house, thinking, "This is my home," yet when that house is consumed by fire, he abandons it and flees because he loves his own body. This case is exactly the same.

The five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*) and so forth are all maintained by other masters; therefore, they are refuted one by one. The Chen translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Furthermore, there are others..."
The Master [says]: This Tathāgata maintains that the worldly joy and pleasure (*lokasaukhya*) is the *ālaya*, as previously explained;

herein, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are designated as the *ālaya*. Furthermore, other teachers maintain that pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*) associated with desire is called the *ālaya*.
Still others maintain that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is called the *ālaya*. As...
These masters, being deluded regarding the ālayavijñāna—both through scriptural authority (āgama) and through meditative attainment—form such attachments.
Because they follow the teachings of the Hīnayāna and practice according to the tenets established by those teachers, their positions do not accord with reason.

However, if there were someone who was not deluded regarding the ālayavijñāna and established this consciousness by means of the terminology of the Hīnayāna, that interpretation would be superior. Why? [Because...]

What is most excellent? If the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*) are designated as the *ālaya*, then among the various paths within the miserable destinies (*apāya*), in those places of exclusively painful sensation where one is born, these appropriated aggregates are most loathsome and contrary; it is within these appropriated aggregates [that the *ālaya* resides].
It is entirely unlovely. It is unreasonable for sentient beings to find joy in it. Why is this?
The sentient beings therein constantly wish for the cessation of the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*) so that they do not arise again.

If this pleasant feeling were associated with desire (*kāma*), then from the fourth dhyāna up to the higher realms, this feeling would be absent; yet if a person has attained this feeling, it is because they seek it.
Regarding the higher realms, one gives rise to revulsion; therefore, it is not logical for sentient beings to find joy and pleasure therein.
If this were the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), then those within the True Dharma who believe in and delight in non-self would not cherish it, nor would they give rise to joy and pleasure therein.
This *ālayavijñāna* is grasped by sentient beings as their own internal self; if it were to arise as something exclusively...
Within the path of painful feeling, one vows that the aggregates of suffering shall be eternally extinguished and never arise again.
However, because the *ālaya-vijñāna* is bound by self-love (*ātma-sneha*), one has never previously aspired to the joyful destruction of the self.
Even for sentient beings born from the fourth dhyāna upward who do not delight in the feelings of desire, there still exists within their *ālaya-vijñāna* this self-love.

It follows along and does not depart. Furthermore, although those within the True Dharma aspire to and delight in non-self and oppose the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), they still possess self-love (*ātmasneha*) within the ālayavijñāna.
Because of this attachment, the names used by various masters for their inferences do not correspond to their actual meanings.
If one adopts these names, the inference regarding the "supreme" (*parama*) would likewise have a name that does not accord with its meaning.

Because it is consistent, citing the names established therein to establish the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is most excellent. This concludes the three preceding citations from the authoritative scriptures (āgama).
Having cited the scriptures, one should now manifest the correct reasoning (yukti).

Concluding the preceding section and initiating the following: Part Four, "The Exposition of Correct Principles," has eleven sections: 1. The mind that maintains the seeds; 2. The ripening mind (*vipākacitta*); 3.
The substance of the realms of existence and birth; 4. That which is appropriated (*upātta*); 5. The triad of life-force, warmth, and consciousness; 6. The mind at the time of death and rebirth; 7.

The basis for the dependent origination of the projecting [factors]; 8. The drawing forth of the food of consciousness; 9. The drawing forth of the mind in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); 10. The drawing forth of defilement.
Purifying the mind. (11) Summary:
As the sūtras state regarding affliction and purification, the mind that sustains the seeds must necessarily exist as a distinct entity.

This [section] on the mind that sustains the seeds is divided into two parts: first, establishing the correct meaning; second, refuting misconceptions. Regarding the first: although it is said to reveal the principle...

Furthermore, one employs scriptural citations of the Buddha’s own teachings and uses logical inference (*anumāna*). Thus, one cites the scriptural definition of "mind" (*citta*) as that which "accumulates and gives rise to":

the scripture states that "it accumulates" because it gathers the seeds of both the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*), and it "gives rise to" because it brings forth defiled and pure manifest activities (*samudācāra*);
therefore, it is called "mind. If the eighth consciousness did not exist, then the "mind that holds the seeds" described in that scripture would be untenable.

Because they must exist. To ensure that the intermittent nature of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) does not contradict the meaning of "mind" (*citta*) as taught in the sūtras, one establishes the following formal argument (*prayoga*):

The seven preceding evolving consciousnesses are the subject (*dharmin*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they are not susceptible to perfuming (*vāsya*) and cannot maintain seeds (*bīja*). The reason (*hetu*) is: [as follows].

Because there are interruptions in states such as the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); because faculties (*indriya*), mental attention (*manasikāra*), and categories such as the wholesome (*kuśala*) arise and cease with ease;

and because they do not abide firmly, they are likened to a flash of lightning. Regarding the phrase "attainment of cessation and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes the five states of non-cognition (*acittaka*).
Regarding the phrase "faculties, objects, and mental attention," these refer to the distinct conditions for the arising of consciousness. Regarding the phrase "categories such as the wholesome,"...
The natures of the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth are also distinct because their categories are each separate; thus, they arise easily and are abandoned easily.

Furthermore, because they are each distinct, the six types of evolving consciousnesses do not necessarily arise together. Because they do not arise together, there is no fixed association (*samprayoga*).

Because there is no association, how could there be an active perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) and a perfumed object (*vāsyam*)? How, then, could they maintain seeds? Only the eighth consciousness is constant and... [is without such distinctions].
It is uniform, stable, abiding, and capable of being perfumed; this accords with the meaning of the sūtra’s statement regarding the mind that maintains the seeds.
To establish the formal argument (*pramāṇa*), one says: This eighth consciousness is the subject (*dharmin*); its being capable of being perfumed is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is:

because it is uniform, stable, and constantly uninterrupted. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like sesame seeds (*tila*) and so forth. "Uniform" excludes those of different types; "uninterrupted" excludes those that are intermittent.
[The eighth consciousness] is severed; it is eternally simple and easy to liberate. It abides firmly, whereas that which does not abide firmly does not.

Next, [the argument] generally infers that if there were no eighth consciousness to receive perfuming, then the defiled and pure active manifestations (*samudācāra*) arising from it would not perfume to form seeds.
Since there would be no seeds, the effort expended in producing those active manifestations would ultimately be rendered fruitless. Why? Because there is no eighth consciousness to receive perfuming.
Therefore, if the first seven [consciousnesses] cannot be perfumed and the eighth does not receive perfuming, there would be no causal seeds.

Since there are no causal seeds, there would also be no manifest fruits; the arising of defilement and purity would thus be causeless. How would this differ from the non-Buddhists' adherence to spontaneous origination (*svabhāva*)?
Next, it is argued that matter (*rūpa*) and the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*) cannot maintain seeds. The formal proof (*prayoga*) is stated as follows:

Form (*rūpa*) is not associated [with consciousness], is not perfumed (*vāsya*), and cannot maintain seeds (*bīja*), because it is not of the nature of mind (*citta*), just like sound, light, and so forth.

This is because form-dharmas are insentient and are non-associated provisional phenomena (*prajñaptidharma*). Next, it is demonstrated that the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) cannot maintain seeds.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows: "The mental factors associated with the evolving consciousnesses are the subject (*dharmin*); they cannot [maintain seeds]..."

The thesis is that [the mind] maintains seeds and receives perfuming. The reason is stated as: because it is easily abandoned and arises [again], because it lacks sovereignty, and because it is not the nature of mind (*cittatva*).
The analogy is like consciousness, which is intermittent; and like mental factors (*caitta*), which—being called "mental factors"—lack the sense of sovereignty and are not the substance of mind.
How, then, could they maintain seeds and receive perfuming? Fourth, since [it is] not...
If it can maintain the seeds, then there is a distinct mind that maintains the seeds; this principle is clear.
Some say that because the six consciousnesses have existed since beginningless time [until they perish], they likewise lack the capacity to maintain the seeds.

The second section, "Refuting the Adherence to [the Notion of] Difference," is divided into four parts. The first part refutes the adherence that the sixth consciousness is the perfumed basis (*bhāvyatā*).

This refers to the Hīnayāna position which maintains that the six consciousnesses and their associated afflictions, such as craving, perfume one another across preceding and succeeding states to form seeds;

it does not depend upon an eighth consciousness. First, the opponent's calculation is presented: regarding the phrase "preceding and succeeding states based on the faculties and objects," this refers to the first six consciousnesses.
There are distinct bases, distinct objects, and distinct acts of attention; furthermore, the afflictions and secondary afflictions each possess their own sequential stages without being intermingled.
Although the entities undergo transformation, there is no difference in their essential nature.
That which is perfumed and that which is capable of maintaining the seeds refers to the fact that although attention, afflictions, and secondary afflictions perform the perfuming...

When one cultivates the various consciousnesses, their perceptions of forms and hearing of sounds are each distinct; yet the nature of these consciousnesses remains identical from beginning to end, without any differentiation.
Thus, the afflictions and so forth act as the perfumers (*vāsana*), while the nature of the consciousnesses acts as the perfumed (*vāsyatva*). Furthermore, it is capable of maintaining seeds.
By means of this, both the causes and effects of defilement and purity are fully established. Why, then, must one insistently establish a separate eighth consciousness?

Regarding the phrase "perfuming and sustaining the seeds," the opponent’s statement that they are non-existent is refuted by the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*). First, he refutes this by distinguishing between the conventional and the real.

He asks: "Is that which you call the 'category of consciousness' real or conventional? If it is real, it is identical to the [views of] the non-Buddhists (for they maintain that the *pradhāna* and *prakṛti* are all substantially existent).
If it is conventional, then it lacks superior efficacy; how could a conventional dharma sustain a real seed? Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

It is said: If it is established that the eye-consciousness arises and ceases simultaneously with afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as greed, and that seeds are formed through the perfuming (*vāsanā*) by those [afflictions] and not by anything else;
then, once this eye-consciousness has already ceased and been interrupted by other consciousnesses, both the perfuming and its substratum (*āśraya*) would no longer be equivalent.
Next, the refutation proceeds according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). First, the refutation of the wholesome (*kuśala*).

The opponent establishes a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows: "If this class of consciousness were of a virtuous or non-virtuous nature, it would not be susceptible to perfuming (*vāsanā*), because it is admitted to be determinate (*vyākṛta*).

It is, for example, like analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). How, then, could it be perfumed? For all instances of analytical cessation are distinguished by being [the result of] the discernment of the virtuous and the non-virtuous.

If, on the other hand, it were of an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature, then these six groups of consciousness would necessarily give rise to the virtuous and the non-virtuous; and at the time when the virtuous and non-virtuous arise, the indeterminate mind..."

If the [defiled] category (*jāti*) is severed, the category should likewise be severed. How then could it receive perfuming? One cannot claim that while the actual entity (*vastu*) may be wholesome or unwholesome, its category remains indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
If the category were indeed indeterminate, it would have to be a distinct category. If it were a distinct category, it would necessarily be a distinct entity.
How can it be established as the perfumed? Because the nature of the perfuming agent and the perfumed must necessarily be identical. Third, refutation by way of interruption:
if it is claimed that the category of consciousness is capable of maintaining seeds, then upon reaching the state of mindlessness, the six evolving consciousnesses have all been interrupted;
since this category would certainly not exist, what would maintain the seeds? And who would receive the perfuming? Fourth, refutation by way of the tainted and the untainted: if it is claimed...

Regarding those types of consciousness capable of receiving perfuming (*vāsanā*): it would follow that for Arhats, perfuming would result in the formation of outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) states, whereas for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), perfuming would result in the formation of outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states.
This is because, since the eighth consciousness is not established, both the noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary beings would equally possess a neutral (*avyākṛta*) type of consciousness.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The mind of an Arhat receives the perfuming of various defilements, because its nature is neutral, just like the mind of an ordinary being. Furthermore, [the mind of an ordinary being]...

A mind arises that receives the permeation (*vāsanā*) of the untainted (*anāsrava*); because its category is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is like that of an Arhat. Fifth, the refutation by means of the mutual permeation of faculties and consciousnesses:

if one claims that there is no distinction between the categories of consciousness, then by analogy with the visual consciousness and so forth, the six faculties—such as the eye—should likewise mutually permeate one another.
The *Saṃgrahaṇī* states: "If one claims that this consciousness is of such a kind that, although they are not associated (*asaṃprayukta*), they are nevertheless identical..."

The various types of consciousness would likewise be able to mutually perfuse one another; by this same principle, other cases would also result in such faults. That is to say, other categories would also have to be treated similarly:
since the sense organs such as the eye are of the same class of pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*), they too would necessarily perfume one another in turn.
This means that the two faculties of eye and ear both possess pure dharmas (*viśuddha-dharma*), and these two purities should mutually perfuse one another.

The same applies to the others. However, you do not accept this; for although they are equally pure dharmas, because they belong to different continuums (*saṃtāna*), they cannot mutually perfume one another.

Consciousness should be treated likewise: although it belongs to the same category of consciousness, how could it mutually perfume itself? The sixth [consciousness] is distinguished by its objective category as previously [stated].
This is refuted later. If it is argued that the substance of a preceding moment perfumes the succeeding moment, thereby establishing mutual perfuming, this is also illogical.
This is because those two moments do not exist simultaneously. Since they do not exist simultaneously, they cannot be in a state of fixed association (*samprayukta*).

Just as one's own thought is separated from another's thought, there is no nature of being either the perfumer (*vāsaka*) or the perfumed (*vāsya*), because [the conditions for] the perfumer and the perfumed...
Because they must exist simultaneously. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The Dārṣṭāntika masters wish to allow a preceding moment to permeate a succeeding moment;
to refute this, it is said that two moments cannot coexist.

There are no two kṣaṇas existing at one time, because there is no nature of permeation through simultaneous arising and simultaneous ceasing. The commentary explains: "Visual consciousness cannot permeate visual consciousness."
Why is this? Because at one time, two visual consciousnesses cannot arise simultaneously. If they do not arise simultaneously, there can be no simultaneous cessation;

therefore, the principle of perfuming (*vāsanā*) is not established. Consequently, visual consciousness and the others are not perfumed by the various afflictions, whether great or small, such as desire, nor are they perfumed by consciousnesses of their own kind.
To establish this through formal reasoning (*pramāṇa*), it is stated: "The six consciousnesses are [distinct] entities and categories..."
They do not mutually perfuse one another, because the preceding and succeeding moments do not coexist, just as they are separated by an interval.

Your assertion that the six consciousnesses function simultaneously and thus serve as the perfumed nature (*bhāvyamāna*) and the holder of seeds (*bījadhārin*) cannot be established on account of the aforementioned reasoning.

There are those who maintain that within the same category of matter and mind, there is no interval [between them] and that they are not objects of perfuming (*bhāvanā*), as has already been explained.
Second, the refutation of the Sautrāntika masters’ position that matter and mind arise sequentially from their own respective categories without depending on the eighth consciousness.
First, the opponent’s view is stated: they maintain that the matter of a preceding moment can serve as the seed for the matter of a subsequent moment.
It arises dependent upon that; the preceding momentary mind can serve as the seed for the subsequent momentary mind and its associated mental factors (*caitta*), which arise dependent upon it.

In this way, the relationship of cause and effect is established. It is not necessary for [the seed] to be perfumed (*vāsita*). Why, then, insist on postulating the *ālayavijñāna* as the cause of all phenomena?
Therefore, what was previously stated—that "mind" (*citta*) is so called because it accumulates (*cita*)—is established as the basis for both the defiled and the pure.
The argument regarding seeds is refuted as being unestablished through both prior censure and subsequent critique. Seeds arise from perfuming (*vāsanā*) and attain growth;
since within their own category there is no sense of a perfumer or a perfumed, no seed or manifest activity can be obtained.

How, then, can one maintain that the former serves as the seed for the latter? If there were no seeds, then that which is interrupted should not arise again, as in the case of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
When one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the realm of form, the principle that the seeds of the former form can produce the subsequent form cannot be established,

because the seeds of form have long since been extinguished and no longer exist. Likewise, when the mind of perception arises after passing away from the non-percipient realm, or when the mind arises upon emerging from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and other such states,
it is likewise unreasonable to claim that the seeds of the former mind can produce the subsequent mind, as these have long since been extinguished.

Because there is no seed in the absence of mind. If one maintains that the matter and mind of the preceding moment serve as the seeds capable of producing the matter and mind of the subsequent moment, then Arhats of the two vehicles would lack subsequent aggregates and could never attain *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, because the two causes—matter and mind—would have been permanently severed.
This is because they do not take the eight consciousnesses as seeds, but rather [take them] at the point of death...
Since matter and mind serve as the seeds for what follows, if neither matter nor mind exists at the moment of death, by what could the subsequent aggregates be produced?

Furthermore, who could then realize nirvana without remainder? It is simply not understood that while there may be the condition of immediate contiguity (*samanantarapratyaya*) between preceding matter and succeeding matter, or between preceding mind and succeeding mind, the condition of cause (*hetupratyaya*) does not exist. Nor should one insist upon [the reality of] matter and mind [in such a state].
These two types of phenomena arise through mutual seeding of one another. Material phenomena cannot permeate seeds in the mind, nor can mental phenomena permeate seeds in matter;
this is because, as in the case of the preceding sense organs and consciousnesses, they do not mutually permeate one another.
Some say that if all phenomena of the three periods of time exist [simultaneously], then all causes and effects cannot be established.
This refutes the Sarvāstivāda school’s tenet that all phenomena of the three periods of time are substantially real (*dravyasat*) as the nature of cause and effect:
namely, that past phenomena act as the cause that brings about results, while present phenomena are the results toward which they tend. Present...

That which is capable of inducing [an effect] serves as the cause; that which is to be reached in the future serves as the fruit. Thus, the causes and fruits of the three periods of time naturally induce and reach one another.
Why then labor to separately postulate an eighth consciousness to maintain the seeds? The Mahāyāna objects, saying: "If there were no eighth consciousness capable of maintaining the seeds..."
For what reason does the Sūtra state that "the mind is designated as 'accumulation' (*cita*) because it can maintain seeds"? To this, the answer is given:
The Sūtra states that the mind is the seed because it possesses the strongest power to produce all defiled and pure phenomena;

therefore, it is said that the mind can maintain seeds. First, [the opponent's position] is refuted. Next, a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute it: The past and the future do not exist as real entities (*dravyasat*). They are not...
Because they are constantly manifest, like flowers in the sky and so forth. Furthermore, the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states:
"The past and future are not of the nature of causes and conditions, because they lack functional activity, like flowers in the sky and so forth.

Since the past and future do not belong to the present, and furthermore are not permanent phenomena (*nityadharma*), and moreover lack the capacity to produce, how could they be grasped as direct generative seeds that give rise to all phenomena? Therefore, it is known that...
If there were no eighth consciousness to maintain the seeds, then momentary arising and ceasing would be mutually unrelated;
by what means could all causes and effects be established?
Some who uphold the Mahāyāna principle of the emptiness of the elimination of signs [hold that] that very mind is this eighth consciousness.

Fourth, there is a class of Mahāyāna bodhisattvas who adhere to the emptiness doctrine of the *lakṣaṇa-vināśa* (destruction of characteristics) school and deny the existence of the eighth consciousness.

Their so-called "inference" is actually not valid cognition (*anumāna*). The Master of the Treatise refutes them, saying: "Sentient beings are attached to signs and are deluded regarding the true principle.
The Buddha taught the dharma of emptiness to dispel that attachment. Fools, not understanding it as a therapeutic antidote, instead cling to that which was meant to be discarded."
The emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) is the ultimate dharma. Relying on fallacious inference (*tarka*), one is unable to understand it correctly;
thus, one denies the existence of this consciousness as well as all phenomena. This contradicts and subverts the various Mahāyāna sūtras cited previously.

Consequently, one claims there is no wisdom capable of severing [afflictions], no delusions to be severed, no fruit to be realized, and no cause to be cultivated—there being nothing but mere verbal expression.
It cannot be so obtained. Would this not contradict and harm the holy teachings, constituting a great false view? Why is this?

For even though non-Buddhists disparage the cause and slander the fruit, they do not claim that these are entirely non-existent like the horns of a rabbit; rather, they merely hold that cause and effect are not substantially real.
If one were to claim that birth-and-death, nirvana, and all dharmas are entirely without substantial reality, the Bodhisattva would not—

One should sever the illusory cycle of birth and death, diligently accumulate the provisions for that which is like a dream or a shadow, and aspire to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, which is like a flower in the sky.
For example, if someone wished to eliminate an illusory enemy, yet employed the son of a barren woman as their army—who among the wise would carry out such a task?
Therefore, one should offer this exhortation to inspire faith. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) states: "Failing to realize the true maturation..."

Those who follow the Vijñaptimātra school mostly cling to the view that the conventional exists while the ultimate is non-existent, forcefully giving rise to divergent opinions and failing to understand the secret intent of the Buddhas.

They grasp at the principle of the emptiness of the elimination of signs as being the final goal; however, this merely destroys the emotional attachments of parikalpita-svabhāva and is a protective negation (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*) intended to prevent errors.

Yet they go so far as to repudiate both *paratantra* and *pariniṣpanna*, treating them all as mere appearances like flowers in the sky. If the bases of *paratantra* and *pariniṣpanna* did not exist...
Consciousness and all phenomena are entirely without intrinsic nature; since they are not substantially existent, [to deny them] constitutes a great false view.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that there is a ripening consciousness (vipāka-citta), and that very mind is this eighth consciousness.
Second, the resultant consciousness (*vipāka-citta*). The preceding seed-holding consciousness is defined in terms of its cause, whereas this resultant consciousness is defined in terms of its fruit.

This resultant consciousness is the eighth consciousness (*aṣṭama-vijñāna*). That is to say, with good and non-good [karma] as causes in a previous life, one brings forth and attains the present-life eighth resultant consciousness as the fruit.
First, a scriptural passage is cited as proof; if that were absent, etc., [it would follow that] the eighth [consciousness] must be established.

Regarding the *vipāka-citta* (maturation-consciousness): it is as stated below. Next, [the author] refutes that the eye and other [sensory consciousnesses] are not maturation-consciousness, establishing the following formal argument (*pramāṇa*):

"The various consciousnesses of the eye and so forth are not maturation-consciousness, because they are intermittent and because they are not the fruit of karma at all times, just like flashes of lightning and the like.
Furthermore, he establishes another formal argument: "Maturation-consciousness should not be interrupted and then resumed again, for such a phenomenon does not exist."
It is like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Since the life-faculty is neither severed nor resumed, it is known to be a maturation (*vipāka*). Question:

The six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, also possess a portion of good and evil that is summoned by completing karma (*pūrṇakarma*); these are called "fulfilling fruits" (*pūrṇaphala*) and are the primary agents of individual retribution.

Why are they not considered maturations? Answer: To establish this through formal reasoning (*pramāṇa*), one says: That which is produced by karma among the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, exists [as a maturation].

The thesis is that this [mind] is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) but is not a true maturation (*na vipāka*). The reason is: because it is not a continuous stream. The example is like sound and so forth.
Therefore, one knows that there must certainly exist a true maturation mind which, as a retribution for projecting karma, serves as the sovereign of the aggregate retribution;

it is pervasive and uninterrupted, internally transforming into the body and externally transforming into the vessel-world, acting as the support for sentient beings and causing all sentient beings [to abide therein].

The internal depends on the body of the faculties, and the external depends on the receptacle world. Since it is logically impossible for the body and the receptacle world to exist apart from the mind, if this mind did not exist, who would transform the body and the receptacle world?
Non-associated formations (viprayukta-dharma) lack substantial reality and therefore cannot undergo transformation.

Furthermore, the various evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna) do not exist constantly; thus, they also cannot undergo transformation. If this mind did not exist, upon what other dharma could [the world] constantly depend?
The establishment of formations dissociated from sentient beings refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character of a group (*nikāyasabhāga*).

Below, this is refuted by means of bodily sensation (*kāyavedanā*). Furthermore, when ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are in meditative absorption and lack discursive thought, the body becomes pliant and they experience pleasant sensation (*sukhavedanā*);
if they are not in absorption and possess distinct discursive thought, the body becomes fatigued and they experience painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*).
However, that this body gives rise to feelings of suffering and pleasure is entirely due to the eighth consciousness (ālayavijñāna) appropriating this body.
If the eighth consciousness did not appropriate this body, how could there be such bodily sensations in those states?

Otherwise, it would not be the case that after emerging from meditative concentration the body experiences well-being, while after emerging from non-concentration the body experiences exhaustion and injury; for apart from the Buddha, no others...
Regarding those in states that are wholesome or unwholesome: it must necessarily be the case that a true resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*) is currently present to sustain this body.
Lest one object: "If that were so, then when a Buddha gives rise to a wholesome mind and so forth, a true resultant consciousness would necessarily be arising at that time."
Consequently, a body experiences a state of physical well-being and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Therefore, this commentary states:
"If one were to allow that a Buddha possesses the arising of *vipāka* (maturation), he would not be a Buddha, but would be subsumed under the category of sentient beings (*sattva*).

Since *vipāka* has already ceased after the vajra-path, the Buddha’s stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) is able to sustain the experience of the body. This [point] is not mentioned here because it is not urgent. From this point downward...
This concludes the preceding argument.
Furthermore, since the sūtras state that sentient beings undergo transmigration [until they reach...], we know that this eighth consciousness exists as a distinct entity.

Regarding the essence of the realms, destinies, and births of the three worlds: while the previous section clarified the mutual retribution of cause and effect, this passage speaks of the essence of those destinies and births; for it exists.
Cause and effect must possess a substantial entity; therefore, this is discussed next. First, a scriptural passage is cited as proof: "If there were no... and so forth.

Next, it is established that the eighth consciousness is the entity of the destinies and modes of birth (*gati-yoni*). This is stated in: "It is necessary... and so forth. Following this, it is demonstrated that the preceding seven consciousnesses are not the entities of the destinies and modes of birth.
That is to say, the eighth consciousness serves as the entity for the three realms, nine stages, five destinies, and four modes of birth. If this consciousness did not exist, then all...
Sentient beings (*sattva*) should not exist [as such]. However, the substance of the destinies (*gati*) and births (*upapatti*) must possess four characteristics:

first, substantial existence; second, permanence; third, universality; and fourth, non-confusion. The eighth [consciousness] possesses these four characteristics and can therefore be established as the truly real destiny and birth.

Regarding "non-confusion," it means that the respective maturations (*vipāka*) of self and other do not intermingle. If there were no true maturation that fully possesses these four characteristics...

Dharmas constitute the substance of the destinies and births; if other consciousnesses were established [as that substance], then the substances of the destinies and births would all become confused, because while abiding within the dharmas of a human destiny born from a womb, one might suddenly give rise to the dharmas of another destiny or another birth. Next, it is argued that material phenomena (*rūpa*) are not the substance of the destinies and births.
As for various resultant material phenomena, they are the neutral (*avyākṛta*) results induced by the sixth [consciousness] through wholesome or unwholesome karma.

The color of mature fruit, as well as a portion of the indeterminate resultant matter produced by wholesome and unwholesome karma within the first five consciousnesses, do not all pertain to rebirth in the realms of existence (*gati*).

This is because such matter does not exist in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Next, it is inferred that the two types of wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) are not the substance of the realms of existence.
Regarding those wholesome states acquired at birth: they are so called because, having previously cultivated them as causes and conditions, one subsequently [arises] therein.
That which is acquired immediately upon birth is called "innate virtue" (*sahaja-kuśala*). It does not depend on cultivation for its accomplishment, as it is inherently present within one's nature.

As the *Renwang Huguo Banruo Jing* (Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for Protecting the State) states: "At the very first moment of a sentient being’s consciousness, they differ from wood or stone; there is innate goodness and innate evil. Evil is the basis for immeasurable unwholesome consciousnesses, while goodness is the basis for immeasurable wholesome consciousnesses. In the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, two categories of wholesome factors are taught, including thirteen types of wholesome dharmas:

first, "virtue by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-kuśala*), which refers to the eleven mental factors beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), up to the thirteenth, "virtue by outflow" (*niṣyanda-kuśala*). Here, "innate virtue" corresponds to the seventh category, "virtue acquired at birth. What is meant by innate virtue? It refers precisely to those [factors].

Regarding all wholesome dharmas: because of prior habituation, one obtains such a retribution; by virtue of this intrinsic nature, one spontaneously and effortlessly dwells in delight in that very state without the need for deliberation.

That which is wholesome as a result of karma refers to that which was obtained through having cultivated wholesome karma in the past. Although these two types of wholesomeness extend throughout the various realms of existence (*gati*), they are not confused with one another;
rather, they are characterized by interruptions and do not exist as a single, constant category. Furthermore, they do not belong to [a specific] realm of existence (*gati*) exclusively.

Because these [realms] must be traversed as mere conceptual designations (*prajñapti*), they lack the status of truly existent entities. Only the resultant (*vipāka*) mind and mental factors possess the four characteristics;
therefore, they constitute the actual, real progression into rebirth (*gati*). The following section deduces the essential nature of this progression into rebirth:

if these resultant phenomena did not constitute the essence of the progression into rebirth, then for one born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) who gives rise to a defiled or wholesome mind, such states would all be identical to the fruit of Buddhahood.
It should not be a realm of rebirth (*gati*), because it lacks the substantial entity of a ripening (*vipāka*) realm of rebirth.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "If one were born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and were devoid of ripening, then defiled and wholesome minds would have no seeds;

defiled and wholesome minds would have no support. (Regarding "defiled and wholesome minds": they are called "defiled" because they consist of the relishing of meditative absorption (*āsvādana*), and they are called "wholesome" because they possess meditative attainments [*samāpatti*]). Furthermore, regarding that very [formless realm]: if...

When the supramundane mind (i.e., the untainted mind) is manifest before one (i.e., when the untainted arises), all other mundane minds (i.e., the tainted) are completely extinguished (all are eternally ceased).
At that time, one should then be liberated from those realms of existence (because the maturation [vipāka] comprised by those realms no longer exists;

one should naturally attain *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* without effort, as the antidote is present and all that is to be countered is eternally severed). Even if it were granted that the essence of birth in a realm of existence comprises tainted seeds—
If one born in the formless realm (*ārūpya*) were suddenly to give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind within a tainted (*sāsrava*) state of mind, all those mundane minds would then cease.

Consequently, the very basis for birth in that formless realm would be abandoned without effort, as the resultant (*vipāka*) emptiness subsumed under *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* would be spontaneously realized.
This is so if one grants the possibility of [the untainted arising] in the formless realm.

Regarding the claim that the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is empty [of being the basis of rebirth]: this would contradict the fact that only the Buddha alone is devoid of the substance of rebirth into a realm of existence (*gati*).

If one does not establish the ripening consciousness as the substance of rebirth into a realm of existence, one commits the aforementioned faults of being neither pervasive nor constant; furthermore, one commits the fault of there being no rebirth into the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If, however, the ripening consciousness is established [as the basis], none of these faults arise. For this reason, the Buddha is not subject to rebirth into a realm of existence.
Why is this? Because the Buddha possesses no dharmas that are *vipāka* (maturation) or neutral (*avyākṛta*). Nor is he subsumed under the realms (*dhātu*). Why is this?

Because the realms are with outflows (*sāsrava*), whereas the Tathāgata’s outflows have been eternally exhausted. The realms consist of causes and fruits; these are the truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*).
Since the World-Honored One has already abandoned the truths of suffering and its origin, the realms—meaning causes—are the seeds of the outflows. All...
Because the Buddha has eternally severed the seeds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the Tathāgata does not belong to the realms of rebirth (*gati*).
All others are subsumed within the essence of the realms of rebirth. Thus, the passage beginning with "Hence we know" concludes the preceding argument.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "There is a body possessing sense organs" (extending until) "that mind is precisely this eighth consciousness.
There are four [points] regarding what is appropriated (*upātta*). Because it is appropriated, it is mentioned next. First, a scriptural proof is cited: "If there were no... and so forth.
Next, the eighth consciousness is established as the appropriating mind. This refers to sentient beings within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
There are the five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and the five internal objects; these constitute the eighth consciousness’s own direct objective aspect (*sākṣāt-svabhāga-viṣaya*).

Only the eighth consciousness is capable of appropriating (*upādāna*) them. If it were any other consciousness, it would lack this capacity. As for the "five material sense-faculties," these refer to the *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate sense-faculties);
their physical bases refer to the *pratibimba-indriya* (conventional sense-faculties). Because past and future phenomena have already ceased or have not yet arisen, they are not appropriated.
Because only that which exists in the present possesses substantial reality, it must necessarily be appropriated (*upātta*).
Because it is appropriated, there must certainly be an appropriating mind (*upādātr-citta*). First, one examines the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) as the appropriator;

this ripening consciousness alone is that which is projected by the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—from previous lives. It is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), because it is neither wholesome nor defiled.
Among those in the good and evil realms, there is a certain class [of beings] who are able to maintain a continuous stream of the appropriated body possessing material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*).

Regarding the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) such as the eye-consciousness, they lack the quality of being appropriated (*anupātta*). To address the objection that "the Buddha has no maturation (*vipāka*);

therefore, the physical faculties of the Buddhas should not be appropriated," it is further explained: the phrase "there is no such meaning" is intended to clarify that the evolving consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, [are what is meant by the term].
Consciousnesses do not all possess the same single category or similar meaning.

This does not indicate that only the *vipāka* (maturation) consciousness is capable of appropriation (*upādāna*), for the untainted physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of the Tathāgatas are appropriated by the immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*). Therefore, the term "appropriation" applies to all states.
If this is so, why was it previously stated that only the *vipāka* consciousness of a single category is able to continuously and universally appropriate?

Regarding the statement, "it appropriates the body possessing material sense-faculties," the commentary explains: "However, as for the contaminated body (*sāsrava-kāya*), only the resultant consciousness (*vipāka-citta*) is capable of appropriation.
Therefore, the Sūtra speaks in this manner; it speaks of the contaminated, not the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)."
It is not meant that the untainted form-body (*anāsrava-rūpa-kāya*) of the Buddhas lacks appropriation (*anupātta*).
Next, a formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is established to refute the position that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) lack appropriation. The formal argument states:

"The various evolving consciousnesses and so forth cannot appropriate the tainted form-body, because they arise dependently upon present conditions, like wind or sound. To say they "arise dependently upon present conditions" means they come into existence by relying on present conditions as a basis.
This refers to the nine conditions for visual consciousness and so forth. Next, the non-appropriation of the three natures is refuted. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows:

Those [states] such as the wholesome and the defiled cannot be appropriated, because they are tainted material bodies not induced by karma, just like non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

This is because the three natures are summoned by their own power and are not induced by karma; they are just like the unconditioned state of non-analytical cessation, which is [defined by] its own nature.
Purity is not manifested by the abandonment of afflictions through the power of wisdom. Third, the refutation that those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are not appropriated:

the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is born of maturation cannot be appropriated, because the contaminated physical body is not born of maturation, because it is not a universal support, and because it is not continuous, like a flash of lightning and so forth.
Fourth, the refutation that mental factors (*caitta*) are not appropriated: the formal argument is...

The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states: Mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) are incapable of appropriation (*upādāna*), because they are necessarily associated with the primary consciousnesses (*citta*), just as in the case of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).
Since the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) themselves cannot appropriate, the mental factors of the evolving consciousnesses likewise cannot appropriate.
Furthermore, the five [sensory] forms and the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are also not appropriated. The formal argument for these states: All that possesses form...

The formations dissociated from the faculties cannot take possession of the physical body endowed with material faculties, because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just like space and so forth.
That which lacks an object of cognition—namely, those formations dissociated from the material faculties—is not a cognizing mind;
therefore, it cannot perceive an object. Since it cannot perceive an object, how could it possibly take possession? Thus, one should conclude by clarifying this point below.
That sutra states that the appropriating mind is precisely the eighth [consciousness].
Furthermore, the sūtra states regarding the triad of life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness.

Regarding the five [factors], life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*): it is said that they not only sustain the physical body (*indriya-śarīra*), but also sustain life-force and warmth;

therefore, they are discussed next. First, a scriptural proof is cited. As for the passage beginning with "If there were no... and so forth, it subsequently establishes that the eighth consciousness is the sustainer of life-force, warmth, and consciousness.

Regarding these three—life-force, warmth, and consciousness—according to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) interpretation: "life-force" refers to inhalation and exhalation, which is the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*). "Warmth" is...
The fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) refers to the fact that the physical forms of the earth element, the fire element, and so forth, which are sustained by karma, do not decay or rot.

"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the momentary cognition and awareness of the mind. According to the Mahāyāna interpretation, it refers to the form-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
That which is apprehended by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is called "warmth" (*uṣman*). The seed of this consciousness is called "life-force" (*āyus*), because it is able to sustain consciousness.
The manifesting consciousness is "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) itself. Now, I shall explain this according to the Hīnayāna; only then will the meaning of the treatise become clear.

That is to say, life-force and warmth are a provisional combination of the two great elements of wind and fire. If there were no consciousness to sustain them for a long duration, how could the formations (*saṃskāra*) continue to persist?

Indeed. Because the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are subject to interruption and transformation, they are certainly incapable of constantly sustaining vitality (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*).

As for that which sustains vitality and warmth, if it were not the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*), what else could it be? To establish this through formal logic (*pramāṇa*): the various evolving consciousnesses are the *dharmin* (subject);

the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they cannot be established as the consciousness that sustains vitality and warmth; the reason (*hetu*) is that they are intermittent and transformative. [The pervasion (*vyāpti*) is: whatever is intermittent and transformative is not the consciousness that sustains vitality and warmth. No...
Because it possesses the function of constant maintenance, it is like sound, wind, and so forth. Furthermore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows:

Only the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) can definitely be established as that which maintains life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and cognition (*vijñāna*), because it functions continuously without interruption or transition, just like life-force and warmth. Question:
The Sūtra states that life-force, warmth, and cognition mutually support one another; does this perhaps refer to a cognition that undergoes intermittent transitions?
By what means is it definitively known that [the mind] functions without interruption? The answer is:
The Sūtra states that the three—vitality (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—mutually support one another.

If vitality and warmth were of a single nature and continued in uninterrupted succession, while consciousness alone were to function with interruptions, how could this conform to the principle of these three factors mutually supporting one another? Therefore, by reasoning from this logic:
